en: The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra-dhāraṇī Sūtra (The Scripture on the Secret Adornment of the Mahāyāna), Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of India during the Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter One: The Assembly in the Secret Adornment (The First Chapter of the Assembly in the Secret Adornment).

Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling in the Land of Secret Adornment (*Guhyakapada*), which transcends the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, as well as non-conceptuality; it is a state of sovereign mastery and unimpeded supernormal power over all phenomena. This land is not the sphere of activity for non-Buddhists or those of the two vehicles. He was accompanied by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields—all of whom were practitioners of ultimate contemplation who had transcended the objects of the triple world’s mind, intellect, and consciousness; whose wisdom-born bodies had transformed their basis; who had accomplished the illusory-like *Śūraṅgama* Samādhi and the Dharma-Cloud Samādhi; and who dwelt in lotus palaces free from all forms of existence, having been personally consecrated by the hands of immeasurable Buddhas. Their names were as follows:

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who served as their leaders were: the Bodhisattva Crusher of Heterodoxies, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Seeing Reality as It Is, the Bodhisattva Sustaining Progress, the Bodhisattva Moon of Liberation, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva King of Supernatural Powers, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha; such were the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who stood at the head.

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, arose from the samādhi known as Manifesting Various Forms through the Eloquence of Supernormal Powers—which dwells in the bliss of the present dharma within the realm of his own realized wisdom—and emerged from the Hall of Sublime Adornments with the Light of Rainbow Lightning. Accompanied by the bodhisattvas, he entered the Palace of the Stainless Moon Treasury and ascended the lion throne in the Secret Adornment Arena, where the assembly of bodhisattvas also took their seats.

When the assembly had taken their seats, the World-Honored One gazed out in the four directions; from between his eyebrows, he emitted a pure radiance called "Adornment of the Topknot Jewel," which spread forth immeasurable light that interlaced and reflected all around to form a net of light.

When this net of light radiates its illumination, the signs of adornment in all buddha-fields appear with distinct clarity as if they were a single buddha-field; the subtle and exquisite decorations of the remaining buddha-fields become like fine motes of dust.

The Ghanavyūha Buddha-field transcends all other Buddha-lands; it possesses neither sun, moon, nor the various stars, and like the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not composed of atoms.

Within this Ghanavyūha, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as those from other lands who have come to this assembly, are all like nirvāṇa, space, and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

At that time, after the World-Honored One had manifested the various lands and the supreme merits of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he again surveyed the assembly of Bodhisattvas in the ten directions with his Buddha-eye and addressed the Bodhisattva Yathābhūta-darśin, saying:
"Yathābhūta-darśin!
This present land is named Ghanavyūha.

Within it, bodhisattvas from the realms of form, formlessness, and non-conception, through the power of samādhi, kindle the fire of wisdom; they incinerate craving for form as well as ignorance, transform their basis of existence, and thereby attain wisdom and meditative concentration.

The mind-made body is adorned with the supernormal powers of the divine feet; it is without apertures or gaps and devoid of skeletal substance, like the sun, moon, rainbow, lightning, purple-gold, bright pearls, crystal, coral, *haritāla*, *campaka* flowers, peacock feathers, the moon, or a reflection in a mirror. Abiding in the various stages (*bhūmi*), having purified the causes of outflows through mastery over samādhi, and having attained the ten ultimate vows and dedications, they have obtained this sublime body and come to dwell here.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Yathābhūta-darśin rose from his seat amidst the great assembly; he bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, bowed with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I now wish to ask a question; I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately grant me leave to speak.
The Buddha told him:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it for you.
At that time, Yathātathādarśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Is it only this Buddha-field that transcends the realms of sentient beings in the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as the realm of non-perception?
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."
Above this place, passing beyond ten billion buddha-lands, there are the Buddha-land of Brahma-sound, the Buddha-land of the King of Śāla Trees, and the Buddha-land of the Star-King.

Beyond such lands, there are further immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lands, vast, exquisite, and adorned with various ornaments. Within them, all the Buddhas expound for the bodhisattvas the ultimate Dharma of the realm of internally realized wisdom—the dwelling in happiness in the present life—which is free from all conceptualization, and which is the true suchness, the limit of reality, and the realm of great parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, you should know that outside of this buddha-field, there are such immeasurable buddha-lands as these. Yathārthadarśin!
It is not only you who now have doubts and wonderings regarding the buddha-fields and the assemblies of bodhisattvas, and thus question the Tathāgata.

There was a bodhisattva named Dhāraṇīśūra who, having once conceived a sense of doubt and wonder in the presence of the Buddha, ascended to the upper realms by means of his supernormal powers. He passed through hundreds of thousands of billions of buddha-worlds, even as many as the sands of the Ganges River, yet he could not see even the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.

A sense of wonder arose in his mind as he contemplated the inconceivable nature of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; he returned to the city of Śrāvastī in the Sahā world, came before me to repent for his transgressions, and praised the Buddha’s boundlessness as being like space, before dwelling in the realm of internal realization and arriving in the Land of Sealed Purity.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, who was well able to expound the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*), having thoroughly and decisively fathomed their profound depths, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, bowed with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"I wish to ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, about a small matter; I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain it for me.
The Buddha said, "Vajragarbha!"
"If you wish to ask me anything, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall comply with your mind and expound it for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, having received the Buddha’s permission, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
What is the meaning of the term "Buddha-enlightenment" (*buddhabodhi*)? What is that which is awakened to?

Please explain the realm of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and reveal the Buddha-nature (*dharmatā*), so as to remove from those currently on the stages of practice their views of formal characteristics (*nimitta*) and their grasping at external treatises. They engage in the discrimination of objects, giving rise to various views such as those of atoms (*paramāṇu*), primal matter (*pradhāna*), the Lord (*īśvara*), time, direction, space, the self (*ātman*), the mind (*manas*), and the conjunction of sense-faculties and objects. Furthermore, they harbor attachments to ignorance, craving, and karma; to the eye, form, and light; and to contact (*sparśa*) and mental attention (*manasikāra*). With these factors acting as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), immediately preceding conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), consciousness arises through their conjunction. Through false conceptualization, they give rise to various discursive arguments concerning existence, non-existence, and so forth.
Within this Dharma, there are furthermore those who fall into the view of emptiness regarding the aggregates and sentient beings.

To sever such false conceptualizations, we pray that the World-Honored One will explain the meaning realized by the Great Bodhi of the Buddha—the one who possesses supreme mastery over all phenomena—which is free from the five kinds of characteristics known by consciousness, so that those who hear it may understand and realize these five kinds of objects of knowledge and thereby attain perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha,
saying: “Excellent, excellent, Vajragarbha!”

Having attained mastery over the ten stages and transcended the realm of conceptual discrimination, you possess great wisdom and desire to manifest the supreme yoga of the Buddha-lineage, which is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

It is not only you who, regarding the meaning realized within the Buddha’s enlightenment, have conceived this rare thought and questioned me; there are also immeasurable bodhisattvas, such as Bhadramāyākāra and others, who all conceive this rare thought toward this same meaning and seek the essence of the Buddha through various reflections:
"What is the meaning of the term 'Tathāgata'?"
Is form the Tathāgata? Or is the Tathāgata something other than form?

Thus, when one searches internally and externally among the aggregates, elements, bases, and all conditioned phenomena, the Tathāgata is not to be found, for all these are phenomena subject to destruction and disintegration.

By means of wisdom and a concentrated mind, one examines with thorough scrutiny; even when analyzing down to the finest atoms, nothing at all is perceived, because the aggregates (skandhas) are coarse and vulgar, whereas the Tathāgata is the eternal Dharma-body.
Excellent, Son of the Buddha!
You are able to skillfully enter the profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*).
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha replied: "So be it;
I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! The Tathāgata, the Supreme Sovereign of the Vajrasamādhi-garbha, is neither the aggregates nor different from the aggregates; he does not rely upon the aggregates nor does he not rely upon them; he is neither arising nor ceasing; he is neither wisdom nor the object of knowledge; he is neither the sense faculties nor their objects.”

Why is this? Because the aggregates, elements, sense bases, faculties, objects, and so forth are all coarse and vulgar; one should not abide in the internal nor abide in the external to perceive the Tathāgata.

"Good son! Form has no sensation and no volition; having arisen, it must perish. It is like grass, trees, tiles, or stones, a collection of subtle particles as insubstantial as a mass of foam on water."
Feeling arises from the conjunction of two factors, like a bubble, a jar, or a garment;
perception likewise arises through the causal conditions of the conjunction of two factors, like a mirage in the heat.

For example, when the heat of the earth rises and billows upward, and it is illuminated by the sunlight, it appears like waves upon water; then various birds and beasts, driven by thirst, see it from afar and perceive it as real water.
Perception is likewise: it has no intrinsic nature and is false and unreal.

For one with analytical wisdom, it appears as if there were an inherent nature, and its distinct characteristics and names can be apprehended; yet for one who observes with meditative concentration, it is seen to be like a rabbit’s horn or the child of a barren woman—merely a provisional name with no initial real meaning.

Just as forms seen in a dream are merely false perceptions of thought that cease to exist upon waking, so too within the dream of ignorance one perceives various forms such as men and women; yet upon attaining perfect enlightenment, there is nothing to be seen.

For example, just as a plantain tree has no core once its layers of bark and leaves are removed, so too is conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*): apart from the body and its objects, it has no essential nature.

Consciousness is like a magical illusion, false and unreal; it is like a magician or a magician’s apprentice who, using grass, wood, and other materials, conjures up humans and various forms of elephants and horses, complete with all their ornaments. These are merely delusions for the greedy and ignorant, not for those of true wisdom.

Consciousness is likewise: depending on others, it abides and undergoes diverse discrimination, arising as the two aspects of grasper and grasped; yet if one understands this for oneself, they both turn and cease. Therefore, it has no substantial reality and is identical to a magical illusion.
“Vajragarbha! The Tathāgata is eternally abiding and forever immutable; this object of the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Just as space cannot be destroyed or extinguished, it is called the realm of nirvāṇa and also the *dharmadhātu*.”
Because all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, present, and future, have taught in accordance with this.

Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, this nature is ever-present; it is called the "nature of the abiding of dharmas" (*dharmasthititā*) and also the "nature of the *dharmatā*."
Vajragarbha! Why is it called *niyamana*?
Because one is completely free from all future evils.
Furthermore, this samādhi can definitively eliminate all evils of future existence; for this reason, it is named *niyamā*.

Should anyone abide in this samādhi, their mind will have no lingering attachment toward sentient beings, as they realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and nirvāṇa—just like hot iron cast into clear, cool water.
All bodhisattvas relinquish [realization] without personally attaining it, remaining merely in close attendance;

they constantly act for the benefit of sentient beings, never abandoning diligence, great compassion, and the perfections, nor severing the lineage of the Buddhas, nor treading the paths of externalists or the two vehicles.
Like a mighty elephant, they are not submerged by the mud of samādhi, and their minds—
Relishing the realm of consciousness, one never regresses in approaching the gateways of the Buddha-dharma;
through ultimate wisdom, one enters the Dharma-body of the Buddha, manifesting the vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata.

One shall attain perfect enlightenment and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma, taking the manifold colors of the cognitive realm as sustenance, entering the concentration of the Tathāgata and roaming within the sphere of nirvāṇa.
Gradually practicing the stages, they transcend the eighth bhūmi; through skillful cultivation, they reach the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā), utilizing the vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgatas.

Abiding in the stage of the Buddhas’ internal realization, they correspond with effortless samādhi (*anābhoga-samādhi*), traveling everywhere throughout the ten directions without moving from their original place, while constantly relying upon the secret [teachings].
He adorns the Buddha-land and transforms his basis; he attains full perfection in wisdom, meditative concentration, mental mastery, the body, powers, supernormal faculties, and sovereign mastery.

Just as the reflection of the moon in the sky appears throughout all waters, so too does the Buddha: he manifests transformation bodies that descend universally upon all worlds. According to the diverse inclinations of sentient beings' minds, he causes them all to receive benefit, ensuring that none who see him do so in vain, and further leads them to eventually reach the Land of Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha).

According to their inclinations and desires, he gradually guides and entices them by describing all the abodes of bliss, such as the Mani palaces of the sovereign Bodhisattvas and the kings of the desire realm, up to the successive merits and adornments of the Buddha-lands in the ten directions throughout the various stages, manifesting himself in response to their capacities until the end of the future.
Just as those who possess mantra-vidyā, añjana-herbs, or the palaces of various rishis may dwell together with humans yet remain invisible,
so too is it when the Tathāgata has completed the deeds performed through his transformations and abides in his true body, remaining hidden and unmanifest.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The aggregates of the sense-faculties are like a cluster of snakes;
Contacted by the conditions of objective spheres, They arise through delusion, craving, and karma; The bonds of habitual tendencies are difficult to untie.”
The mind and its mental factors are restless and ever-unsettled;
entangled by applied and sustained thought, they are like dragons coiled together.
From this, the poison of hatred arises, like a fiercely blazing fire.
All those who practice contemplation, in order to relinquish the phenomena of the aggregates,
should constantly and truthfully contemplate this with single-minded diligence, free from laxity;
it is like the shadow in the midst of empty space, which exists though there is no tree.
To see the tracks of birds in the wind or their footprints on the road is difficult;
likewise, to perceive the Tathāgata within the phenomena of form and non-form, whether created or created by another, is equally difficult.
Suchness, the limit of reality, and so forth, as well as the essential nature of all Buddhas,
are the sphere of internal realization that transcends the realm of all language.
Nirvāṇa is called the Buddha, and the Buddha is also called Nirvāṇa.
When all conceptualizations are abandoned, how can it be seen?
If a gold ore is ground into powder, no gold is found within the ore;
only when the wise skillfully smelt and refine it does the true gold finally manifest.
When all forms are dissected down to the finest atoms,
and when the aggregates are likewise analyzed for their identity or difference,
the essence of the Buddha cannot be seen; yet it is not that the Buddha does not exist.
One who is in meditative concentration observes the Tathāgata, complete with the thirty-two marks;
if such matters as pleasure and so forth were performed, they would all be clearly manifest.
Therefore, one should not say that the Tathāgata does not exist in meditative concentration.
The Buddha who is the single object of samādhi, the Buddha who is the virtuous cause and virtuous root,
the Buddha who is supreme in all worlds, and the Buddha who is the Perfectly Awakened One—
these five kinds of Buddhas are real; all others are merely emanations.
The thirty-two marks of excellence are fully present within the Tathāgatagarbha;
therefore, the Buddha is not non-existent, for those who possess meditative concentration can perceive him.
Transcending the three realms, he dwells throughout immeasurable Buddha-fields.
In the subtle and wondrous land of the Tathāgata, pure Buddha-sons fill it completely.
Meditation and wisdom support one another to form a firm and stable nature;
they roam through the Ghanavyūha realm, contemplating the majestic power of the Buddha.
The beings within the Ghanavyūha are in every way equal to the Buddhas;
transcending momentary destruction, they constantly dwell in samādhi.
The World-Honored One possesses great meditative concentration, remaining profoundly still and in right reception.
Adorned with the marks and signs and all virtues, both internally and externally,
the multitude says that this is a transformation body of the Buddha who descended from Tuṣita;
yet the Buddha always dwells in the Secret Adornment (Guhyasamāja), and these images appear from that realm.
Abiding in truth and entering right concentration, myriad forms arise according to conditions;
like the moon in the void, its reflection is seen in all waters;
like the many images of a mani jewel, they appear clearly as colors blend together.
The Tathāgata abides in right concentration, and his manifestation of forms is likewise so.
Just as a form and its reflection are neither identical nor different,
so too does this Supreme Being accomplish all his activities.
Neither from atoms nor from primordial nature, nor from time, nor from the Lord,
nor from other such conditions is the world created. Rather, the Tathāgata,
by means of the nature of causes, adorns the essence of its fruits.
In accordance with what is appropriate for the world, all things manifest in their various forms;
sporting within samādhi, there is nothing, whether internal or external, that he does not accomplish.
Mountains, rivers, forests, and wilds, as well as friends and all kinsmen—[all appear before him].
The myriad stars, along with the sun and moon, are as bright as mirrors, hanging down in their celestial forms.
All such worlds as these he entirely encompasses within his body;
then, placing them within the palm of his hand, he scatters and tosses them about like mustard seeds.
The Buddha possesses mastery over meditative concentration;
the Muni, the most supreme Honored One, cannot be created by anyone in the world, for he alone is the transformer.
Those who are blind, obscured, and ignorant, rush along in the flow of false conceptualization.
Those who are attached to existence and non-existence, to self and non-self,
or who claim that all things perish, or that only a portion ceases—
such people as these constantly bring harm upon themselves.
How can these various views arise within this? The Buddha pervades the three realms;
he is the Great Teacher of contemplative practice.
He views the world as a city of the gandharvas, and all the manifold activities he performs—
Just like forms in a dream, or the water sought by a thirsty beast,
they advance and retreat due to various karmas, driven by the wind-ropes. The Buddha,
who possesses sovereign knowledge and vision within these skillful means, [perceives them thus].
Just as a skilled artisan skillfully maintains the mechanism of a loom,
or as a master mariner grips the rudder and steers the ship,
so too is the Tathāgata most subtle and wondrous, tranquil and boundless.
Transcending all roots of attachment, it is realized by those with pure faculties.
This is the basis for the subtle and wondrous concentration of those who practice meditative absorption;
it abides within the clear and luminous minds of all practitioners of contemplation.
The Buddha-body is most pure, Neither existent nor non-existent;
It is far removed from all limits And from the duality of subject and object of cognition.
The mind in accord with wondrous wisdom Is the supreme realm.
Knowing that all characteristics are devoid of intrinsic nature—this is seeing the Tathāgata.
With a mind that has shattered all conceptual associations, one does not cling to samādhi;
abiding on the path free from defilement, all things are entirely undefiled.
The devas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, sages, and non-Buddhists praise and make offerings to him;
yet he does not crave or seek after them, but rather engages in the activities of the world.
Abiding in fundamental purity, in accord with the wondrous principle,
those gods and humans who behold him see the manifestations of his transformations;
yet the Buddha does not appear as this or that, but is like the sun and the moon.
Abiding on the path of perfect fulfillment, he manifests the removal of all arrogance;
toward those of various heterodox schools, each different from the others, he guides and restrains them according to what is appropriate.
Through his manifold methods of wisdom—such as the treatises on kingship and the three Vedas—[he brings beings to maturity].
All these are spoken by the Tathāgatas, sustained by the power of meditative concentration.
Whether among kings and their ministers, or even in mountain forests,
all ritual protocols originate from the Buddha.
The treasuries of myriad jewels throughout the ten directions produce pure gems;
all these belong to the God among Gods, due to his sovereign majestic power.
Within all the three realms, there are those of great wisdom.
Various karmic activities through diverse skillful means are accomplished by reason of the Buddha.
Now descending from Tuṣita, surrounded by a host of celestial maidens,
they enjoy themselves together with song and dance, constantly gathering and sporting day and night.
Or like the wise Śreṇika, the householder Śailopa,
who held the straight cord of the world, bestowing and taking away, summoning and releasing;
though appearing as one of clear intelligence in every place, he was nonetheless a fool.
Yet within the Ghanavyūha, all is tranquil and devoid of movement;
this is the realm of the Great Muni, which the ignorant and foolish differentiate in various ways—
like those with cataracts in their eyes, or like a herd of thirsty deer.
Just as one perceives illusions in the world, or all that is grasped within a dream,
so do the sons of the Buddha perceive the realm of the God among Gods in its true nature;
thus does the practitioner of yoga awaken from sleep.
Nara and Īśvara, Brahmā and Śatakratu, Nanda and Kumāra,
Kapi, Śuci, and the others— though they abide in meditative concentration and deliberate with discernment, they remain perpetually deluded regarding this.
In the past, future, and present, all the Munis—
though their minds are veiled by habitual tendencies— are likewise unable to see it.
Excellent, Vajragarbha!
Furthermore, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, you now dwell in the Land of Secret Adornment;
this is your own realm, which I shall now explain for you.
There are those who engage in false conceptualization regarding the Primal Nature (Prakṛti) and atoms (paramāṇu).
Just as when various objects are crafted, their diverse forms and appearances arise as nothing but the arising of dharmas, and cease as nothing but the ceasing of dharmas.
To falsely imagine that all things are produced by subtle atoms is a delusion.
The cause can be known through its effect, just as a lamp illuminates objects.
Its characteristics cannot be apprehended beforehand; likewise, they remain unapprehendable when it later perishes.
Within the past, no substantial entity exists that can be found.
The future is likewise so; apart from conditions, there is no intrinsic nature.
Within each and every condition, one seeks everywhere but finds no essence.
Seeing neither the existence nor the non-existence of a nature, there is also no view of non-existence.
Regarding the aggregates, jars, garments, and so forth, they analyze them with subtle discrimination;
these three hundred and sixty heterodox schools destroy the true path,
causing one to wander through birth and death, where the dharma of nirvāṇa does not exist.

**Chapter Two: The Arising of the Sublime Body (Part One)** At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathatādarśana—possessing great majesty and sovereignty within the world, his body exquisitely beautiful and adorned with superior robes—rose from his seat before the Buddha and stood to one side. Bowing deeply with palms joined, he paid homage with single-minded reverence and addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha as follows:

“Venerable One, you have skillfully attained mastery over the realm of your own wisdom and dwell in the bliss of the present dharma (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*). Your mind is in perfect harmony with the worlds of the three vehicles. You are a master of great samādhi, possessing sovereign power over meditative absorption, and are able to explain the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*) in accordance with reality. You constantly abide within all Buddha-lands, acting as a leader for all to expound the profound and sublime Dharma.”

Therefore, I now entreat the Venerable One to explain the realm of internal realization—the state of dwelling in happiness in the present life—which the noble ones do not follow others in their practice.

May I and the other bodhisattvas behold this Dharma, so that we may practice in peace and bliss, proceed toward the stage of Buddhahood, and fully attain the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*), the speech-body, as well as the powers, superknowledges, and masteries.

"Transforming the basis while not abiding in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), like a mani-jewel of many colors manifesting all forms and images, one explains the practice of the Guhyavajra at all Buddha-fields.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva said:
"Excellent, O Lord of Beings!"
"You have been able to request that I speak on the dharma of selflessness as it enters the Ghanavyūha.
O Lord! You should first realize that all objects of conceptualization are manifestations of the mind, and within those objects, you should abandon all conceptualization."
"O Benevolent Lord!
All worlds are seen through conceptual discrimination; by seeing the essence of the world, one attains samādhi regarding the objects of perception.
I shall now reveal that Dharma King for you; you should listen well."
Then he spoke these verses:
"All worlds are like a mirage in the heat;
By means of unreal characteristics, They are falsely discriminated where nothing exists."
Awakening arises from that which is awakened to; that which is awakened to appears in dependence upon the awakener.
Apart from one, there is no second, just as light and shadow coexist.
When there is no mind, there is also no object; thus, neither the means of cognition nor the object of cognition exists.
Relying solely upon the one mind, one thus makes such distinctions.
Regarding the knowing subject and the known object, one realizes that they are merely the mind’s false conceptualization;
once it is understood that the known object does not exist, the knowing subject likewise is not found to exist.
The mind is the self-nature of phenomena, yet it is turbid for human beings;
upon entering the eighth stage, it attains purity.
In the ninth stage, one practices meditative concentration, and in the tenth stage, one achieves great awakening.
The water of Dharma is poured upon his crown, and he becomes one honored by the world.
The Dharma-body is inexhaustible; this is the realm of the Buddha.
Ultimately, it is like empty space, and the mind-consciousness is likewise so.
Inexhaustible and indestructible, adorned with manifold virtues,
they dwell eternally in the inconceivable, the pure lands of the Śrī-māyādhāraṇī Buddhas.
Just as when a jar is broken, the shards thereby become manifest.
When a tile is broken, its dust is revealed; when dust is analyzed, the ultimate atom (paramāṇu) is revealed.
In this way, by means of outflowing causes (sāsrava-hetu), one accomplishes the outflow-free dharma (anāsrava-dharma).
Just as fire burns wood until it is exhausted, yet continues to burn in another place.
Tasting the wisdom of immovability, they transform their basis and leave behind conceptual discrimination;
within the Land of Secret Adornment, they thus manifest eternally.
Not giving rise to various categories of existence, they do not dwell in the world.
Abandoning all views, take refuge in this selflessness.
Severing the flow of all continuities, where there is neither arising nor destruction,
exhausting all views, take refuge in this selflessness.
All afflictions have been stilled; dwelling in silence, inconceivable, and purified of all views, I take refuge in this selflessness.
The various phenomena of the world are, from the very beginning, devoid of a self-nature.
It is not through being struck or destroyed that it ceases to exist, nor is it revealed by means of a metaphor.
Just as a fire, having consumed its fuel, extinguishes of its own accord therein,
so too does the wisdom that perceives the three realms as selfless.
This is called the bliss of the present life, the domain of the noble ones’ own wisdom;
relying upon this, they enter the various stages, purifying the evils of beginningless time.
Having abandoned worldly dependencies, they dwell securely in the supramundane.
"His mind becomes increasingly pure, / And he dwells eternally in the Land of Secret Adornment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathatādarśana and the assembly of kings all spoke these words: "Vajreśvara!
"We now all desire to take refuge; we pray that you will show us the place of refuge.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha replied in verse:
"The Buddha-body is not existent, Nor is it non-existent; there is no Buddha. "
The tree of the aggregates has been incinerated, and the hosts of Māra have all been utterly defeated;
abiding in the stage of the Tathāgata within the wondrous land of Ghanavyūha,
you possess awakened realization that is pure and stainless— O Lord of Benevolence, you are worthy of refuge.
Far removed from all conceptual constructions, Realizing that which has no location—
To the masters of the Guhyasamāja samādhis, The Sovereign of Benevolence,
you should take refuge. In the supreme, pure realm of Guhyasamāja, The dwelling place of all the noble ones,
"When the practitioners of contemplation are filled [with this], they should take refuge in this adorned land.
At that time, having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha further addressed the Bodhisattva Yathārthadarśin, saying:
"O Lord of Beings!"

Having already attained the stages, those practitioners of contemplation observe all worlds as being like high and low relief in a painting; like the beautiful female forms seen in a dream; like a barren woman suddenly dreaming that she has given birth to a son; like the various activities within a city of the *gandharvas*; like a wheel formed by a whirling firebrand; like hair hanging in the air; like the forms of men, horses, forests, flowers, and fruits produced by illusion; like the shadows of floating clouds; and like the flash of a rushing lightning bolt—all of which are false and not truly existent, produced by conceptual discrimination just as a craftsman fashions a vessel.
O Benevolent Lord!

The habitual tendencies of sentient beings in the world shroud the mind, giving rise to various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). The manas, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the other cognitions evolve in continuous succession, constantly associated with the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*).
For example, when a torrential stream is struck by the wind, various waves arise; these waves follow one after another as the flow continues without ceasing.

The ālaya-vijñāna within the world is likewise: beginningless habitual tendencies are like a torrential stream, which, being stirred by the winds of objective conditions, gives rise to the waves of the various consciousnesses that are forever uninterrupted.
O Benevolent Lord!
Although these eight kinds of mind do not possess such distinct substantial entities, they arise either gradually or simultaneously according to conditions.
When the mind arises and perceives various objects, there is likewise such a distinction between gradual and instantaneous processes.

Regarding such places as houses, the various constellations, military encampments, mountain forests, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits—one generally perceives them either simultaneously or in succession.

If, while asleep or dreaming, one sees what was previously experienced; or if one recollects from birth until old age and death; or if one calculates various objects, investigates the meaning of phrases, contemplates diverse literary styles, or partakes of fine food and drink—regarding these objects, one may understand them sequentially, or there may be those who grasp them all at once.
O Benevolent Lord!
The nature of the mind is fundamentally pure and inconceivable; it is the subtle and wondrous treasury of all Tathāgatas, like gold within its ore.
The mental faculty arises from the mind, and the same is true for the other six; thus, these many varieties are differentiated within the phenomena of the world.
O Benevolent Lord!
Although the ālayavijñāna coexists with the perfuming agents, the mental factors, and even all seeds of defilement and purity, its nature is eternally luminous and pure.

The lineage of the Tathāgata should be known to be likewise: its distinct states of being determined or undetermined are eternally pure, like the ocean which remains constant while waves and tides shift.

The ālayavijñāna is also thus: through gradual cultivation across the stages (*bhūmi*), with their distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior, one abandons all defilements and attains luminous manifestation.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha spoke again in verse:
“Excellent, O you of true wisdom!
Regarding this subtle and wondrous Dharma, having heard it from me, your mind is pure and able to comprehend it.”
In all lands throughout the ten directions, amidst the assemblies of various kings,
you should extensively proclaim [the Dharma] for them according to what is appropriate.
If people, having heard the Dharma, gradually purify the ālayavijñāna,
Sometimes he becomes a king among men, a wheel-turning monarch over the four continents;
or again, he becomes Śakra, lord of the gods in Tuṣita, Suyāma,
and even up to the palace of Vaśavartin, becoming the sovereign of the desire realm.
Some become lords of the form realm, or are born in the formless heavens and among the non-conceptual beings,
experiencing the bliss of various meditative concentrations.
Realizing the Truth yet not dwelling therein, they are like the lion’s roar.
Mastery over all meditative concentrations, In harmony with joy and bliss,
they single-mindedly seek the Ghanavyūha, Unstained by attachment to the triple world.
Having reached the Ghanavyūha, They gradually attain awakening.
Having attained the transformation of the basis, one obtains peace and bliss, dwelling eternally in tranquility.
Surrounded and adorned by immeasurable sons of the Buddha,
one becomes a sovereign king of the Dharma, the most supreme among the assembly.
It is not as the non-Buddhists claim, that nirvāṇa consists in annihilation;
for if it were annihilation, it would be identical to the conditioned, and there would be the fault of death followed by rebirth.
Through the superior, middling, and inferior [degrees] of the ten karmas, the three vehicles arise.
Born supreme in the Guhyasamāja, one advances through the successive stages.
Having attained the wisdom of liberation and the subtle body of a Tathāgata,
why speak of nirvāṇa as a phenomenon of destruction?
If nirvāṇa were subject to destruction, sentient beings would have an end;
if sentient beings had an end, they would likewise have a beginning.
There must be some non-arisen phenomenon that first creates sentient beings.
There is no non-sentient being who is born into the realm of sentient beings.
Once the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, the Buddha has no *jñeya* (knowable) phenomena;
thus there would be nothing to awaken to, nor would there be nirvāṇa.
Those who falsely conceptualize liberation speak of it as liberation,
like a seed that has been scorched, or a lamp extinguished, or fuel consumed.
Their description of the nature of liberation is the destruction of existence and the establishment of non-existence.
Regarding the sublime bliss of liberation, they remain far removed and unable to realize it;
yet in the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the dhyānas, the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and the meditative absorption of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*),
they enter and emerge both forward and backward, possessing mastery over all powers and supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*).
Not retreating from that state, nor remaining perpetually submerged,
they thoroughly know the characteristics of all phenomena and attain skillfulness in the various stages;
thus adorned, they come to the Land of Secret Adornment.
If one says that the nature of liberation consists in destroying existence to establish non-existence,
such a person remains within the various realms of existence and can ultimately never escape them; furthermore,
they destroy the threefold conjunction as well as the four types of conditions, such as the causal condition.
The eye and form as internal and external conditions, the consciousness produced from their conjunction,
and all internal and external phenomena of the world— these mutually arise through reciprocal power;
yet all such manifold meanings are entirely contradictory [to your position].
If one knows that what appears is mere consciousness, And is detached from what is obtained by the mind,
Conceptualization does not manifest before one, Nor does one dwell in its nature;
At that time, free from objective referents, The mind enters a state of tranquil meditative absorption.
Having abandoned within the world the views of the grasped and the grasper,
one undergoes the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) and becomes free from coarse heaviness (dausthulya).
Possessing inconceivable wisdom and the ten kinds of mind-made bodies (manomaya-kāya), one is adorned with manifold wonders.
Having become the sovereign of the three realms, you have come to the Land of Secret Adornment.
Matter and mind, as well as mental factors, the dissociated formations, and the unconditioned—
whether internal or external, mundane or supramundane— when observed with true insight, are seen to be without distinction.
Thus these wise ones come to the Land of Sealed Splendor (Ghanavyūha).
Characteristics, names, and conceptualization, as well as correct gnosis and suchness—those in meditative concentration can clearly illuminate them; their essential nature is entirely equal.
One enters the pure land of Ghanavyūha, praised by the Buddhas.
If one destroys the threefold conjunction as well as the four types of conditions,
one does not remain firm in one's own school and becomes like those of false discrimination.
Those who harbor evil habitual discriminations—those five types of proponents—fail to establish their metaphors; all their arguments are contradictory.
All five incur faults and confuse the eye of wisdom.
Inversion and non-inversion, as well as identity and difference— these categories collapse.
Abandoning one’s own tenets and relying on the doctrines of others,
all views such as the "beginningless limit" arise from this destruction.
Great King, you should know that sentient beings within the various realms of existence revolve like a wheel; their beginning cannot be found.
Out of compassionate vows, the Tathāgata universally responds to all those with whom he has a karmic connection.
Like the light of the pure moon, there is nowhere it does not pervade;
according to the faculties and natures of each, he teaches the Dharma as is appropriate.
If nirvāṇa were subject to destruction, what merit would the Buddha possess?
There are three kinds of *adhicitta*, and liberation is likewise;
the Four Truths and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*); the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);
the four conditions, the formless attainments (*ārūpya-vihāra*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The factors of enlightenment, the various stages, and so forth, as well as conditioned and unconditioned phenomena,
even down to all the noble ones— all exist in dependence upon consciousness.
The knowledge of the nature of suffering, the knowledge of the contemplation of suffering, and the knowledge that arises subsequently to suffering— [all likewise depend upon consciousness].
The same applies to the knowledge of origination; for cessation and the path it is likewise.
These twelve types are called "clear observation" (*abhisamaya*).
There are ten kinds of learners (*śaikṣa*): the eighth [stream-enterer] and those who are reborn seven times at most.
Those who go from family to family, those who attain nirvana after one more interval,
those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state or upon rebirth, those who attain it with effort or without effort,
and those who flow upward through various stages— only then do they enter parinirvāṇa.
In all such ways, the levels and stages of the various wisdoms differ as inferior,
middling, or superior for those who practice contemplative cultivation.
The superior cultivation of the Bodhisattvas is the most preeminent in its meritorious achievements.
From the eleventh and twelfth, up to the sixteenth,
these practitioners of meditative concentration further gradually extinguish the mind.
That which is exhausted is not the mind, nor does it coexist with the mind.
The future mind has not yet arrived; because it has not arrived, it does not exist.
When the conditions for the mind do not harmonize, it arises neither from this nor from that.
In the fourth dhyāna there is no mind, yet its causes cannot be destroyed.
There are causes, namely the various consciousnesses— the mental consciousness and the five sensory consciousnesses—
which, through false conceptualization, fail to realize their own nature, arising like waves.
The one established in meditative concentration observes the ālayavijñāna, free from the discrimination of subject and object.
Subtle and without anything existing, the transformation of the basis is indestructible.
Abiding within the Ghanavyūha, it is ever as radiant as the moon;
there, the wise ones of the Ghanavyūha are always together with the Buddha.
Constantly roaming within the realm of meditative concentration, there is a single flavor without distinction.
This is the abode of those established in the *Ghanavyūha* samādhi; it arises through the power of concentration.
Therefore, one should cultivate the mind that accords with this wondrous samādhi.
Within the six heavens of the desire realm, the twelve abodes of Brahmā and Māra,
the formless realms, and the state of non-perception— among all these stages,
if one is born in the Land of Secret Adornment, one shall become a lord of gods therein.
Those who seek the Land of Secret Adornment Should cultivate the ten kinds of knowledge:
Knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, Conventional knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, And [knowledge of] suffering,
its origin, cessation, and the path, As well as the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
O Benevolent One, you see the truth: the Śāṇakavatsa clan and the Ikṣvāku kings of the lunar lineage are no different in their spiritual descent.
You should seek the Guhyavati realm; do not harbor doubt or let your mind retreat.
Like a sheep being led by force, panting with fear as it retreats,
the mind dwells within the body like a phantom beast;
it is also like a tree conjured by illusion, or like reeds and rushes in a river.
Just as a king sports in a garden, moving about his various limbs,
so too do the mind and mental consciousness, together with all mental factors, arise;
like clouds gathering in the sky, they assemble yet possess no reality.
The seed-store consciousness (ālayavijñāna), entangled and shrouded by various habitual tendencies,
is like a mani jewel that manifests various colors according to conditions;
though it dwells within the bodies of sentient beings, its essence is pure and free from defilement.
This is the definitive lineage, and it is also Great Nirvāṇa.
Names arise dependent upon signs; signs arise from causes and conditions.
Because of various forms and characteristics, conceptual discrimination arises.
Discrimination arises from two causes: external signs and the habitual tendencies of the mind;
one should know that the seventh manas-consciousness is likewise so.
When the sense faculties, the mental faculty, and their objects come together, the five consciousnesses are produced.
The mental factors are in mutual association, thus abiding within the body.
With right wisdom one constantly observes that all worlds arise from such causes and produce their respective effects.
True Suchness is not different from this; all phenomena arise in mutual dependence.
With a mind that accords with principle, one clearly perceives and contemplates this.
This is precisely the ultimate, true nature of all phenomena.
Furthermore, that which is conceptually constructed by delusion— All phenomena are unborn.
The nature of all dharmas is eternally empty; It is neither non-existent nor existent, like illusions, mirages, And the various things such as cities of the Gandharvas.
Various forms and appearances, Names, phrases, and the collection of phonemes—
Through such attachments these arise, Forming the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The union of sense-faculties, objects, and the mind Impregnates [the consciousness] to form seeds.
Indistinguishable from the mind, the various consciousnesses arise from this;
through the power of mutual causality, this is called the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
The wisdom that internally realizes reality is the dharma that abides manifest before one.
This is what is called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the realm of all the sages.
The Buddhas and their spiritual heirs realize this and are thus called "sages.
If a person realizes this Dharma, they immediately behold the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
He proclaims: "Birth has been exhausted; the holy life is fully established.
What was to be done has been accomplished; I am forever free from all states of existence, liberated from all suffering, and have extinguished all fears."
Thoroughly understanding the two kinds of selflessness regarding phenomena and persons,
one universally incinerates all habitual tendencies and forever severs conceptual discrimination.
From beginningless time, these have been accumulated through discursive proliferation.
Immeasurable multitudes of faults and evils— All have been entirely removed.
Just as when a ball of hot iron The heat departs while the iron remains unimpaired, So it is with the liberated one: Delusion is exhausted and they are cool.
Entering the untainted realm, the wondrous land of Ghanavyūha;
this land is most subtle and exquisite, beyond the reach of others.
It is the pure abode where the Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas dwell.
The bliss of samādhi manifests before them, and they take this as their sustenance.
Those who wish to be born in this land should cultivate the contemplation of reality;
furthermore, for the sake of all those with whom they have a karmic connection, they should proclaim it widely according to the principle.
Names arise based on characteristics; characteristics, in turn, originate from conditions.
All various forms of conceptual discrimination exist because of these characteristics.
Roots, objects, vases, robes, and so forth, are all composites formed by the factors of the aggregates.
Discrimination arises from this; through clear understanding, one discerns its distinctions.
Whether moving or unmoving, all worlds arise from the darkness of delusion, having ignorance as their very essence.
Length, shortness, and other forms, sounds, and the realm of odors;
sweetness, bitterness, hardness, smoothness, and so forth—these are the objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Furthermore, phenomena that are wholesome or unwholesome in nature, as well as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, [are likewise its objects].
Even up to nirvāṇa, this is the domain of wisdom.
Moment by moment, all things constantly shift and transform; they all arise in dependence upon consciousness.
It is like the power of a magnet, which attracts iron and causes it to revolve.
One should know that it is likewise with the manas regarding the ālayavijñāna.
Just as a snake may have two heads, each performing its own function,
so too is the defiled mind (kliṣṭamanas), which grasps at the ālaya.
It can perform my activities, increase what belongs to me, and further, in conjunction with consciousness, it serves as the support for its arising and passing away.
Within the body, the sensation of warmth arises; it moves and performs all manner of karmic actions.
Food, drink, and clothing are enjoyed according to their needs;
leaping and dancing, or various forms of self-delight—
all these bodies sustained by sentient beings arise from the power of the mind.
Regarding all objective realms, such as dreams and optical illusions,
one gives rise to various conceptual discriminations, not knowing they are merely one's own mind.
It is like a person in mid-air, performing acrobatic feats on a tightrope.
Tossing about, precarious, and lacking stability—discrimination is also like this.
Having no basis for its own existence, it functions only within its own domain;
like an image in a mirror, consciousness perceives various forms.
This delusion belongs to the foolish, not to those of clear wisdom.
O Lord of Men, you should know that these three are all manifestations of consciousness;
that which is detached from them is what is called reality.
The Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvara and others, as well as the noble Maudgalyāyana,
surveyed billions of lands and saw that they were all adorned with various excellences.
Yet, among those adornments, this land is the most preeminent.
In Sukhāvatī and Abhirati, and even down to the lower regions,
throughout immeasurable billions of lands praised by all the Buddhas,
it is said that the Ghanavyūha realm manifests its majestic power spontaneously.
Without beginning and without end, it is the primordial ground of the Tathāgatas;
transcending the three realms of existence, it is quiescent and free from purposeful activity.
Both self-benefit and the benefit of others have their accomplishments fully perfected therein.

It is not that they do not attain Buddhahood here; yet, while performing Buddha-works within the realm of desire, they necessarily rely on the Guhyasamāja (Ghanavyūha) to manifest as immeasurable billions [of forms].
Constantly abiding in right concentration, they sport with the various supernormal powers.
Throughout all lands, like the moon there is nowhere it is not seen;
according to the various classes of sentient beings, he transforms and benefits them as is appropriate.
Through the *Daśabhūmika*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and other [sutras], as well as the Great Tree and supernormal powers, [he brings about this benefit].
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and other scriptures all emerge from this sūtra;
this sūtra is most preeminent, and no other scripture can compare to it.
O benevolent lords and all kings, you should pay it full respect.
The realms of desire, form, and formlessness, and the celestial palaces of the non-conceptual gods—
having already transcended all these, the Buddha dwells in reliance upon the Secret Adornment (Guhyasamāja).
The various palaces of this land are like lotuses, fully adorned with every ornament.
All these Tathāgatas are the sublime manifestations of pure wisdom;
the Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas are ever present within them.
The World-Honored One dwells constantly in dhyāna, the most supreme state of tranquility.
Relying on his own inconceivable meditative absorption, he manifests a multitude of wondrous forms;
these manifestations of form are boundless and cannot be seen by others.
In the land of Sukhāvatī, adorned with supreme excellence, dwells the World-Honored One, Amitāyus.
For all those who practice contemplation, the forms and appearances are likewise so.
Some see the God among Gods, resplendent and imbued with manifold colors:
the hue of *karketana* coral, the luster of pure gold and the bright moon.
Like peacocks, *suvarṇa*, *gokṣīra*, coral, lotuses, lightning, and the like;
or seeing his body emaciated, clad in tattered rags, and reclining upon straw;
or appearing like the light of a thousand suns, seated upon a great lotus flower.
Some see various bodhisattvas with the topknots of dragon kings adorning their heads,
or with crowns of precious gems embellished with indranīla jewels;
some see the marks of wheels and banners, or the various signs such as fish and conchs.
Some see radiant colors, trailing through the sky like a rainbow;
some see Mount Sumeru placed upon their right palm;
or they hold the waters of the great ocean, appearing as small as a cow’s footprint.
In some places he sees himself as a king of men, wearing the ceremonial cap and robes upon the palace veranda,
surrounded by his ministers and attendants, together proclaiming the transformation of the nation.
In other places he sees various bodhisattvas, the most supreme practitioners.
They teach within their own domain the Dharma known by the Buddhas of the past. Or,
through wisdom and meditative concentration, they swiftly transform the basis,
attaining a body like an illusion that is entirely unimpeded in its various manifestations.
Some demonstrate the full understanding of objects, severing all karma of grasping and attachment;
having eliminated all views, they no longer undergo further existence.
Like a lamp whose oil and wick are exhausted, it goes out and enters nirvana.
Some manifest the practice of all the pāramitās,
the great assemblies of the Mahāyāna, providing for others without end,
as well as ascetic practices, the observance of precepts, and various other ritual rules.
In the Land of Utmost Bliss and Adornment, beings are not born from a womb;
their physical forms are like pure gold, and their radiant colors are ever-perfect.
These masters of yoga possess both bliss and luminosity.
The realm of such persons does not possess even one hundredth part of this.
Those among the people of Sukhāvatī naturally obtain food according to their thoughts;
the Victorious Muni’s supreme mastery is surely the flavor of nectar.
There are precious trees named "As You Wish," beneath which one may roam and rest;
exquisite gold is ground into powder and strewn upon the ground as adornment.
Ponds of lotuses and various flowers bloom in full splendor, their buds opening wide.
Thus fully adorned, there is nothing that can serve as a metaphor.
If a person possesses pure faith, skillfully practices the various meditative concentrations,
delights in the Buddha's virtues, and applies themselves with single-minded dedication toward dedication (pariṇāmanā), [they shall attain this].
"Immediately within the Buddha’s supreme land, One is born through transformation upon a lotus flower, Adorned with all the marks of excellence, Brilliantly clear and free from dust or stain.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, having spoken these verses, manifested his own body as being the size of a finger joint, or like a mustard seed, or even a hundredth part of the tip of a hair; or he manifested the body of a Buddha, or the body of a Pratyekabuddha, or the body of a Śrāvaka, as well as immeasurable other various forms, while preaching the Dharma.

It is further said that when a bodhisattva enters the various stages (*bhūmi*), they thoroughly understand the five dharmas, the eight consciousnesses, the three natures, and the two kinds of selflessness. Attaining the illusion-like samādhi, they assume bodies at will; possessing sovereign supernormal powers and fearlessness, they never regress and purify their basis of reliance. Thus they enter the stage of Buddhahood, where the untainted aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are eternal and immutable.

It is said that the Bodhisattva is skillfully able to traverse paths such as a dream, a reflection, or the moon in water—the path traversed by practitioners of contemplation—who have attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and a body like the ten illusory metaphors; whose ultimate vows are all fulfilled without exception, who have reached perfect enlightenment and sit upon a wondrous lotus flower, surrounded by the assembly of all Buddha-sons.

Some say that by the power of their vows, bodhisattvas manifest various forms to travel through all lands and serve successive Buddhas; these bodhisattvas possess bodies so subtle and wondrous that they exist neither in being nor non-being.
For example, the hosts of celestial sages and gandharvas who dwell upon Mount Sumeru or in the void cannot be seen by beings who travel upon the earth.
Those bodhisattvas are likewise; they cannot be perceived by those who practice meditative observation.

Alternatively, it is said that because the Bodhisattva has attained the power of the samādhi of mastery over dhyāna, he manifests birth and parinirvāṇa within lotus palaces in the lands of the ten directions.

It is said that by the power of samādhi, the Bodhisattva transforms the basis of existence yet does not abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); in all places where sentient beings exist, he manifests various bodies, his mind being as impartial as the earth, water, the sun, and the moon.

Alternatively, it is said that with a mind of great compassion, the Bodhisattva takes pity on all sentient beings who wander through birth and death, impoverished and lowly, oppressed by manifold sufferings. Just as a black bee alights upon a ship and travels across the great ocean, drifting with the vessel for one *yojana* or even for hundreds of thousands of immeasurable *yojanas*, [the Bodhisattva] preaches for them that there is no self and that birth and death are impermanent, causing them to know that things are extinguished swiftly and do not abide for even a single moment.

Some say that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas see all sentient beings deluded by craving and thirst, oppressed by the suffering of conceptual discrimination; within the signless Dharma, they grasp at signs and falsely cling to the existence of grasper and grasped. This grasper and grasped entangle their minds, causing them to drift incessantly in the ocean of birth and death, impoverished, solitary, and without refuge, like a spider’s web in the midst of the great sea.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are like those who remain on a boat; out of compassion for all sentient beings, desiring to bring them liberation from the hardships of birth and death, they manifest their bodies according to what is appropriate for each and teach various practices such as giving.

The Remainder of the Second Chapter,
"The Arising of the Sublime Body. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra-Vividha-Rūpa-Mahāprabha,
together with his peers— the Bodhisattvas Lokadhara, Vīradhara, Mañjuśrī, and Abhijñārāja— [proceeded].
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the noble Bodhisattva Candra, the Bodhisattva Vajrāṅkuśī,
the Bodhisattva Mahāvṛkṣarāja, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, and others, including immeasurable devas from the Maṇiratna Palace,
the assembly of Buddha-sons within the Land of Secret Adornment (Guhyakaprabhāsā), and those who had come from other buddha-fields to hear the Dharma.
Having heard the teaching on the subtle and wondrous merits of the *Ghanavyūha*, they developed profound respect for the Dharma;
having attained the definitive transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), they dwell eternally in this land and are never born elsewhere.
Nevertheless, out of compassion for future sentient beings and wishing to bring them universal benefit, they united their minds and addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, saying:
“Venerable One! Please explain this to me.”
Who created the various forms and images of all the worlds?
Are they fashioned like a potter who kneads clay to create jars and other such worldly objects, or is it not so?
Furthermore, just as when a performer strikes strings, bamboo, gourds, and wood, a complex sound is produced through their convergence, is it not the same for all things in the world?

If each individual thing possessed three intrinsic natures (svabhāva), would the manifested forms and characteristics of all worldly objects already exist within a single object, even those that have not yet come into being? How could they all possibly reside within one thing?
Is it for the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Mahāvṛkṣa Kiṃnaras?
Or is it for Subhūti, the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the Brahmā Śikhin, and the Formless Heavens?
Is this created by all these lords of the gods acting with one mind and united effort?

Or is it that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of this and other realms produce all these various forms of the world through their power of transformation, causing delusions to arise therein—delusions that are seen like water in a mirage?

For example, just as a jar serves as the locus for its qualities, so too all things in the world that abide in a locus are not themselves bound to those qualities, nor do the qualities depend upon the qualities; rather, through their successive conjunction, the collection of various qualities is formed.
Regarding these various forms and images in the world, are they merely delusive confusion, or do they have a stable existence?

Some say they were created by Mahābrahmā, Nārāyaṇa, or Maheśvara; others claim they were produced by the self-power of Kapila or the Ṛṣi Kaṇāda; while still others falsely maintain that they arise from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), spontaneity, time, ignorance, craving, or karma.

All the celestial sages and all others who practice worldly meditative concentrations harbor doubts: Is it that there is no substantial reality, being like a phantom, like a dream, like a mirage, or like a city of the Gandharvas; that beginningless conceptualization has produced the grasped and the grasper, like a two-headed serpent, like a walking corpse, or like a wooden man moved by a mechanism, or like hair hanging in the air, or a whirling firebrand?
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha replied in verse:
"The various forms and images in the world Are not produced by a creator;
They were not made by Kuvera, Nor by Indra and the others."
Nor is it the fruit of merit from great assemblies of giving or sacrificial offerings;
nor is it the cause taught in the Vedas, for those are mutually contradictory and lack definitive meaning.
Yet it is not non-existent either, for it is capable of sustaining the causes of the world.
What is called the ālaya, the eighth consciousness of the person,
moves within all things, like a wheel turning out various jars,
like oil pervading sesame seeds, and like the salty taste inherent in salt.
Just as the nature of impermanence pervades all forms,
and as musk and deer-musk possess fragrance, so too do the light of the sun and moon;
they are neither creator nor created, neither existent nor non-existent.
Far removed from all non-Buddhist paths, And from various views such as oneness or difference;
It is not sought by means of ordinary intellect, And cannot be analyzed through conceptual discrimination.
That which is realized by internal wisdom Is the unimpeded state of a concentrated mind.
If one were apart from the ālayavijñāna, there would be no other consciousness remaining.
Just as waves in the ocean are not different from the ocean itself, yet while the ocean remains still, the waves come and go; thus they cannot be said to be one and the same.
For example, as one who cultivates meditative concentration,
with a mind purified by internal stillness and mastery over the supernormal powers,
can perceive all the various forms of higher knowledge through the practice of contemplation— this is not something understood by others.
The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is likewise; it functions together with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Buddhas and the sons of the Buddha, as well as those established in meditative concentration, constantly perceive it.
The storehouse consciousness sustains the world, just as a thread strings together beads.
Just as a chariot has wheels that turn according to the wind of karma,
and as a potter turns his wheel with a staff so that vessels are formed for various uses,
so too the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and the various realms work together with power such that there is nothing they cannot accomplish.
Throughout all worlds, both internal and external, it pervades and encompasses them entirely.
Like the multitude of stellar constellations arrayed across the void,
sustained by the power of the wind, their movement proceeds without ever ceasing.
Like the tracks of birds in the sky, though sought they cannot be seen;
yet the birds do not leave the sky as they soar and wheel, advancing and retreating.
The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is likewise: it does not depart from one's own or another's body.
Like waves rising upon the ocean, Like the sky containing the myriad phenomena,
So too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), Storing all habitual tendencies (vāsanā).
It is like the moon reflected in water, And like various lotus flowers.
Just as water is never separate from itself, yet is not defiled by it, so too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which cannot be stained by habitual tendencies (vāsanā).
It is like having a film on the eye: the eye can never see itself.
The storehouse consciousness dwells within the body, Encompassing and storing all seeds;
Pervadingly sustaining life-force, warmth, and cognition, Like clouds covering the world,
its karmic functions never cease, Yet sentient beings are unable to perceive it.
The world’s false conceptualization perceives that oxen and the like possess horns;
failing to realize that horns do not truly exist, it asserts that rabbit horns are non-existent.
When analyzed down to the subtlest atoms, not even a trace of a horn can be found.
One must depend upon existent dharmas to give rise to the view of non-existence;
yet since existent dharmas are fundamentally non-existent from the start, what could the view of non-existence possibly depend upon?
Whether as existent or non-existent dharmas, they are mutually dependent upon one another in turn.
Within the two dharmas of existence and non-existence, one should not give rise to conceptual discrimination;
if one is detached from the object of cognition, the cognizing subject does not arise.
It is like a whirling firebrand, or various phenomena such as optical illusions and phantoms.
All arise because of limited perception, giving birth to these various cognitions;
if one is separated from their causes, these cognitions do not exist at all.
Names and forms are mutually bound, and habitual tendencies are without end.
All conceptual discriminations arise together with the mind;
when the true reality is realized, the mind of habitual tendencies no longer arises.
From beginningless time, one has been submerged and deluded by various false objects.
Through the habitual perfuming of conceptual proliferation, various kinds of minds arise.
The grasper and the grasped are the intrinsic nature of the sentient being's mind;
forms such as jars and garments do not exist apart from the mind.
All is nothing but cognition; the objects of cognition do not exist at all.
The nature of the cognizer and the cognized naturally evolves in this way.
The habitual tendencies disturb and cloud the mind, such that the ignorant and foolish are unable to see it.
Just as when struck by the wind, the waves of the ocean never cease;
so too, when the mind is stirred by the winds of objects, the waves of consciousness arise.
Through various kinds of conceptual discrimination, one grasps from within oneself.
Just as the earth is without discrimination, yet all things depend upon it to grow,
so too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) the locus of dependence for all objective realms.
It is like a person using their own hand to rub and grasp their own body.
Just as an elephant uses its trunk to take up water and sprinkle itself,
or as infants place their fingers in their mouths,
so too do objects appearing within one's own mind become the very conditions for that same mind to perceive them.
This realm of the mind pervades the three realms of existence;
those who have long practiced contemplative cultivation are able to thoroughly penetrate that all internal and external worlds are manifestations of mind alone.

At that time, having finished speaking these words, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha sat in silence, abiding in a subtle dhyāna that has no fixed location; he roamed through the gates of the Dharma-realm and entered the sphere of all Buddhas. Seeing that there were immeasurable sons of the Buddha who would come to this land to dwell upon the stages of cultivation, he arose from his concentration and emitted a great radiance, which universally illumined the palaces of the gods of the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, and the heaven of non-perception.

Within this radiance, there further appeared immeasurable, most excellent buddha-fields, adorned with the infinite marks and signs of the Buddhas. According to the desires and inclinations of all worldly beings, they brought them benefit, causing them all to receive and uphold the name of Ghanavyūha.
Those sons of the Buddha looked at one another and spoke these words:
"The Buddha-land of Ghanavyūha can purify all merits and extinguish all sins; it is the dwelling place of those who practice contemplation, and among all Buddha-lands, it is supreme and peerless."
"Upon hearing his name, our hearts are filled with joy; let us go together.
Thereupon, the sons of the Buddhas each came to this land from their respective abodes.

At that time, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and the Brahmā King Śikhin of Akaniṣṭha gathered in one place; they all conceived a sense of rare wonder toward the Buddha and the bodhisattvas of this land and addressed the Brahmā King, saying:
“O Lord of Devas!
We all now give rise to this thought:
‘When shall we be able to attend upon the Heavenly King as he proceeds to the Land of Secret Adornment?’”
At that time, having heard these words, the Brahmā King immediately set out together with the host of devas; however, midway they hesitated, not knowing where to go.
The Brahmā King first attained realization and reflected thus:
"The Pure Land of Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha) is the realm of contemplative practice; if one is not the right person, by what means can it be reached?"
"This is not a place that can be reached by the devas of the desire, form, or formless realms, nor by the supernatural powers of non-Buddhist practitioners; how then have I come here?
He further thought to himself:
"Perhaps the God among Gods has lent me his majestic power so that I may arrive here so swiftly."
Having formed this thought, he uttered a cry of refuge. Immediately, he saw immeasurable Buddhas appearing along the path, their majestic radiance shining brilliantly.
Then the Brahma King Śaṅkhakuṇḍala addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What should we do now so that we may swiftly proceed to the Buddha-land of Ghanavyūha?
The Buddha told them: "You may return."

Why is this so? Because the Land of Śrī-vaśa is the realm of contemplative practice and the dwelling place of those who have attained right concentration; it is the most supreme and peerless among all Buddha-fields, and cannot be reached by those who possess form.
When the Brahmā Śikhin heard the Buddha’s words, he and the assembly of devas immediately returned to their celestial palace.
At that time, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens deliberated among themselves, saying:

"The Brahmā Śikhin possesses great majestic power, yet he was unable to go there; one should know that this land is most preeminent, being the sphere of activity only for practitioners who have attained the Illusion-like Samādhi."
Thus, as the praises of the merits of Ghanavyūha resounded, they were heard everywhere by all who came to this assembly.
Having heard these words, the sons of the Buddhas present there felt even greater joy and reverence, and addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha:
"We harbor a deep longing for the Dharma; we pray that you, O Great Illuminator, will proclaim it for our sake."
Vajragarbha said: "Who could fully expound the Dharma taught by the Buddha,
except for those who are protected and sustained by the Tathāgata?"

The Tathāgata possesses supreme mastery over contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), and his entire sphere of experience is inconceivable; how could he possibly provide instruction or exposition for those who are not practitioners of contemplation?
Then the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvara, along with the sons of the Buddha such as Suyāma and others, again spoke with one voice, requesting: "Please speak quickly!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Abhijñārāja, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Kiṃnara, and a multitude of other immeasurable bodhisattvas also spoke these words:
"Excellent, O worthy one!"
"Please grant us this teaching swiftly.
At that time, there were also immeasurable devas in the void who played celestial music and joined together in their exhortation.
Then, Brahmā Śikhin, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic power, came to this assembly and addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha in verse:
"This great assembly today is adorned with such unprecedented splendor;
they are all the Venerable One’s disciples, wise and peerless.
All of them, in the presence of the Venerable One, thirst for and long to seek the Dharma."
I still do not yet know what it is you ask; are you asking about Kaurava,
or about Vijaya and Mūrdhaja, or even about the horse Aśvakarṇa, and the deeds performed by the Wheel-turning Kings?
Do you ask about the Ikṣvāku lineage, or the kings who wielded a thousand bows?
Do you ask about the dharmas of humans and devas within the realms of desire, form, and formlessness?
Or do you ask about the conduct of Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas?
Even unto the asuras and the various treatises on the stars and celestial phenomena—
may you please explain these matters in their proper sequence. We,
together with the devas, shall all listen with single-minded devotion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha addressed the great assembly:
"Have you not heard how the Brahma King Śikhin, the hosts of the Śuddhāvāsa devas, and the sons of the Buddha have all earnestly requested this Dharma?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, the Bodhisattva Lokadhara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvara, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin, the Bodhisattva Devagarbha, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, and other countless sons of the Buddha who had come together from billions of lands, all gazed upon the Honored One Vajragarbha and spoke these verses:
"The pure wisdom of the Tathāgatas of the past and the future— The Honored One received this directly from the Buddhas; He understands it clearly and has no doubt in his mind."
