"This assembly all delights in hearing it; we pray that the Honored One will expound it at this time.
Then, Vajragarbha, the King of Samādhis, surveyed the great assembly and replied in verse:
"The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is not something I am fully able to expound."
Except for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who are protected by their majestic spiritual power,
I now pay homage with a sincere heart to the Buddha and all his sons within the sovereign, pure palace and the chamber of the maṇi-jewel treasury.
I speak out of a heart of reverence; the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom perpetuates the lineage of the Buddhas. You all should listen and receive it.
This is not a discourse on the past and so forth, but the supreme Dharma of the kings.
It is shown only within the Guhyasamāja as the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
The Buddha’s wisdom is exceedingly subtle; it is the supreme merit of the Muni, the practice of correct contemplation, and free from all mental conceptualizations.
Therefore, it is not by my own power that I can expound this profound [teaching], but solely through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority that I have heard and received it from the Buddha.
This wisdom is most subtle and exquisite; it is the flower of all samādhis.
The Buddha, dwelling within the Ghanavyūha, Expounds the teaching while in meditative absorption.
He is far removed from all verbal expressions And from all views,
such as existence and non-existence— These four kinds of extremes.
This is called the most pure, the wondrous principle of the Middle Way.
Those practitioners of the Śrī-vaipulya-dharmadhātu-samādhi who are able to contemplate this,
having abandoned attachment and achieved the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), swiftly enter the stage of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the assembly of sons of the Buddha, having heard these words spoken by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, bowed their heads in reverent homage and addressed him, saying:
"We have conceived a profound love and delight for the Dharma, like one parched with thirst longing for water, or like a bee yearning for honey."

Now, the assembly of sons of the Buddha within this gathering have all attained mastery over profound meditative concentration and wisdom; possessing great supernormal powers, they rule over all worlds, and they wish to hear the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.

I only pray that the Venerable One, with a Brahma-like voice, a voice like that of Indra, and the profound sound pleasing to all the Tathāgatas, shall expound this supreme meaning so that it may be clearly understood.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
“The meaning of the words spoken by the Tathāgata is truly real, rare, and difficult to perceive.
For example, it is extremely rare to see the shadow of trees and other objects in the sky where no such things exist; likewise, the teaching of the Tathāgata is equally rare.”
Just as no one is able to see the wind in the sky or the tracks of a bird, so too it is with the various meanings and intentions taught by the Muni, which are likewise difficult to perceive.
Regarding the phenomena of the world, those possessed of wisdom can explain them clearly through analogies;
yet that which is proclaimed from the Buddha’s own mouth transcends all analogies and is beyond the reach of words.

What I perceive is like a dream or a city of Gandharvas; those practitioners of meditation present here in this assembly possess great wisdom and have already attained clear understanding of the true meaning.
How can I now explain the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas for such a person?
Nevertheless, I shall, relying upon the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, proclaim and describe it for the sake of the assembly.
"You sons of the Buddha, you should all listen attentively.
What the Tathāgata has spoken accords with both letter and meaning; it transcends mind and intellect and is beyond the reach of analogy.
It is like a cluster of exquisite flowers where swarms of bees compete to gather nectar: those that arrive first take the finest essence, while those that arrive later taste only what remains."
"In this way, the Tathāgata has attained the refined essence of the Dharma; I taste its remainder and speak it for the sake of the assembly.
He then spoke these verses:
"The realm of the God among Gods Brings increasing joy to those of clear wisdom."
Beyond the reach of mind or speech, it cannot be described through measurement or discrimination.
Desiring to universally subdue the prideful minds of the world,
he manifests a human form, adorned with the marks of a Buddha.
The halo and the wheels upon his feet, all these various marks are fully perfected;
as he dwells and travels through the various palaces, he is gazed upon by both humans and devas.
Throughout the four seasons, the Tathāgata always abides in the Secret Adorned Realm (Ghanavyūha).
Throughout all worlds, he manifests birth and parinirvāṇa.
When the time of pure goodness has diminished, amidst the arising of evil and the turbulence of the defilements,
he benefits each class of sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them.
Karmic activity never pauses, yet the Ghanavyūha is eternally unmoving;
the stainless realm of Ghanavyūha is the support for those who practice contemplation.
When evil arises and the age is turbid and chaotic, it manifests the marks of the Tathāgata.
Just as the pure, full moon Reflects its image throughout all waters,
So too do these various forms and images Appear everywhere throughout the world;
Such is the realm of the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom, Which is perceived by those who possess true knowledge.
Because the various classes of sentient beings have diverse inclinations, the Buddha manifests through various bodies, responding and transforming according to what is appropriate.
Some see him as Maheśvara; others see him as Viṣṇu.
Some see Kāpilavastu dwelling in the void preaching the Dharma;
some see Vidyādhara, or again see Nitya-cārī; some see Śāntanu, Kumāra, and Śikhin.
From Rāhu and the Kṛttikās, down to the Kiṃnaras,
and the kings of the Ikṣvāku and Lunar lineages— all who look up to and revere him;
from diamonds and other precious gems, down to lead and tin.
All arise through the Buddha’s majestic power, appearing according to what is appropriate.
Celestial maidens, nāga maidens, and gandharva maidens approach with refined composure, yet they cannot disturb his mind.
The Tathāgata has already subdued all objects within the desire realm;
it is likewise with the form and formless realms—none can delude or disturb him.
Even those in the various meditative absorptions of non-perception have not yet escaped the entanglements of affliction.
Neither peaceful nor pure, one falls away and wanders in saṃsāra.
Born from those who possess a body, it is not like the Land of Secret Splendor (Ghanavyūha);
the subtle and wondrous land of Secret Splendor is adorned with pure merit.
The person possessing the knowledge and vision of liberation is the most supreme refuge;
endowed with the ten kinds of great mastery, the powers, the superknowledges,
and the dharmas of samādhi, they are adorned like a Buddha, possessing a wondrous body born of the mind.
Practicing the ten stages, with the perfections such as generosity,
adorned with the various marks, their bodies are exceedingly pure.
They are far removed from conceptual discrimination, yet it is not that they lack awareness.
Free from the conceptualizing mind-faculty, the faculty of wisdom is ever joyful.
Through the perfection of all pure deeds, such as generosity and other virtues, one attains the Buddha’s supreme support: the pure land of Ghanavyūha.
This land is most subtle and wondrous; it does not rely on the sun for illumination.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas extend their radiance to shine everywhere.
That light is exceedingly majestic and brilliant, surpassing a hundred thousand suns.
There is no distinction between day and night, nor is there the affliction of old age and death;
in the most excellent realm of Ghanavyūha, all the devas look up with longing.
The supreme practitioners advance through each stage of the bhūmis.
Having realized that all phenomena Have the mind as their very nature,
And having skillfully explained the ālayavijñāna, The three natures, and the selflessness of phenomena,
Their bodies have become utterly pure, And they have come to be born in this land.

**Chapter Three: On Womb-Birth (Middle Section)** *The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Chapter Three: On Womb-Birth At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha again addressed the Brahmā King Śikhin, saying:

"Lord of Devas, you should know that the bodies of sentient beings are composed of nine substances as their nature. These conditioned characteristics are constantly shifting and changing; they are aggregates of the great elements, various forms, and subtle atoms, synthesized from impure semen and blood, and perpetually enveloped by immeasurable karma."

It is like a poisonous tree, luxuriant and dense, in which greed, hatred, and delusion grow together; after nine or ten months have passed, driven by the power of karma and moved by the impulse of life, it emerges headfirst from the birth canal, oppressed by distress and affliction, undergoing immeasurable suffering.
"Lord of Devas!

These sentient beings have come to be born here from among humans, or from among animals, hungry ghosts, rākṣasas, asuras, and so forth; some were once universal monarchs or even possessed sovereign power and majesty among the gods; some were mantra-holding non-Buddhist seers along with their retinues; and some were practitioners of dhyāna who fell away from meditative concentration—it is from such places as these that they are born here."

Once born, as the sense faculties grow and mature, one creates various karmas according to the causes and conditions of past habits and associations; furthermore, due to these karmas, one wanders through the various realms of existence.

If there are those of wisdom who encounter virtuous friends, hear the Dharma, and through contemplation attain realization; who do not cling to words and texts and remain free from all conceptual discrimination; who enter the three gates of liberation and perceive the true principle of phenomena—most supreme, pure, and supremely, most supremely pure—they shall come to dwell in this Buddha-land of Ghanavyūha, manifesting themselves as appropriate throughout immeasurable billions of Buddha-fields.
"O Lord of Devas!

One who is thus born shall forever attain liberation from the perilous realms of birth and death; such a person is called a 'great man' (puruṣa), is called a 'wise one,' and is further described as the 'God among Gods,' surrounded by the assembly of all the sons of the Buddhas."
"Lord of Devas!
The body within the womb is false and unreal; it is not born of intrinsic nature, nor is it produced by ignorance, craving, or karma. Why is this so?"

They exist through the causal characteristics of ignorance, craving, and karma; if one can thoroughly comprehend them so that they are all extinguished without remainder, such that even names and conceptual discriminations no longer exist, this person will be born in the Land of Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha).
"Lord of Devas!

If those who are concentrated dwell in samādhi, yet their minds have objects of attachment, they will be deceived and deluded by forms and sounds; thus giving rise to grasping and attachment, they cannot remain steadfast. This is precisely what is called the path of distraction."

If the power of this samādhi arises within the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, or even among the beings of the sphere of non-perception, that person is then bound by that very samādhi.

If one abides in samādhi, skillfully taming the mind so that it is free from the grasped and the grasper, and once these two graspings have ceased, the mind no longer arises; such a person is called a practitioner of true contemplation.
"If you wish to be born in the Land of Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha), you should always abide in this Samādhi of Reality.
Chapter Four: Manifesting One's Own Works, from the Mahāyāna Ghanavyūha Sūtra. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha again addressed the Brahma King Śikhin, saying:
"O Lord of Devas!..."

The mind has eight or nine types which, together with ignorance (*avidyā*), serve as the cause of the world; the entire world is but the manifestation of the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

These minds and mental factors, along with the sense faculties, undergo birth, cessation, and cyclic flow, being transformed by ignorance and the like; yet the fundamental mind remains firm and unmoving.
"Lord of Devas!

The dependent origination of the world consists of twelve factors; whether they be faculties or objects, the producer or the produced, they all perish in each moment. From the Brahma-world up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception, everything arises through dependent origination; only the Tathāgata is free from all dependent origination."
"Lord of Devas!
All phenomena within and without the world, whether mobile or immobile, have the nature of disintegration and destruction, just like a jar and such things.
Lord of Devas!"
The various consciousnesses undergo subtle, rapid, and swift transitions; this is the realm of the Buddhas, not something that can be known or seen by the world’s sages or non-Buddhist practitioners.
Ensnared by craving, these sages and non-Buddhists are unable to comprehend the distinctions among the characteristics of the mind.
"Lord of Devas!

Suppose there were someone who, with diligent resolve, performed sacrifices to the gods by chanting and praising the Vedic rites for one month, or for a full four months, or likewise for one year up to a thousand years; even if they were born in the Brahma realm, they would ultimately return to decline."
Lord of Devas!
Do you not know? The fruit obtained through the practice of the three Vedas is, for example, like the nature of the plantain tree—lacking solidity.

Lord of Devas, the Ghanavyūha Buddha-field is the place of liberation for all Tathāgatas; it is attained through wisdom and meditative concentration. If you desire liberation, you should practice it well.
"Lord of Devas!

Those within the Guhyasamāja (Ghanavyūha) have no affliction of kinsmen or the cycle of birth and death; their minds are not stained or attached by the habitual tendencies of various karmas. Like a lotus flower emerging from the water, like space free of dust, and like the sun and moon rising high and pure without clouds, they are constantly sustained by all Buddhas. Bathed in the stream of pure precepts and drinking the essence of wisdom, they attain true understanding and cross to the shore beyond birth and death."
"Lord of Devas!

Within the bodies of sentient beings, all phenomena such as the elements, the five aggregates, and consciousness are non-existent. Consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions, just as fire blazes forth because of wood."
"Lord of Devas!

All objective realms revolve in accordance with deluded consciousness, like iron that moves and shifts following a lodestone, or like a mirage and the city of the Gandharvas, which thirsty deer mistakenly perceive through their ignorance and delusion."
Within this, there are no such things as a creator or the like; it is merely a transformation of the minds of ordinary beings.
Lord of Devas!

Just as the people in a city of the gandharvas—who come and go, run about, and perform various actions—are seen but not real, so too are the movements, postures, and activities of sentient beings’ bodies; they are like what is seen in a dream, which ceases to exist upon waking.
When people of the world perceive phenomena such as the aggregates, their awakened mind clearly illuminates that they are originally quiescent.
O Lord of Devas!
The collection of subtle particles resulting from the combination of earth and other elements cannot be found at all if separated from the mind.
Among all things in the world that can be held or lifted, which is not a composite of the great elements (*mahābhūta*)?

For example, just as various objects are seen through the delusive confusion caused by conditions such as wind or phlegm disorders, or as a reanimated corpse has no agent behind it, so too are all phenomena in the world.
"You sons of the Buddha should diligently observe this. O Lord of Devas!

All things in the world, whether moving or stationary, are like masses of foam gathered together to form shapes; the perceptions of jars, garments, and the like are identical to a mirage; the various sensations of suffering and pleasure are like floating bubbles; formations (saṃskāra) are like the core of a plantain tree, lacking any solidity; and consciousness (vijñāna) is like a magical illusion—deceptive and unreal."
"Lord of Devas!

Within the three realms, all phenomena—whether mobile or immobile—are like dream-visions appearing to a deluded mind, and like illusory events or a city of Gandharvas that merely deceive the foolish."

If the sons of the Buddha, regarding such a Dharma, are able to correctly awaken to and know the mind with fearlessness, they shall burn away all causes and conditions of affliction with the fire of wisdom and be born in the wondrous and blissful land of Ghanavyūha.
"Lord of Devas!
All worlds are devoid of marks; marks constitute bondage, while the absence of marks is liberation.
Marks are mental objects, and mental objects are not real."
The true Dharma is the domain of wisdom; it is free from all marks and is not within the range of the mind.
Lord of Devas!
All marks are the phenomena of the triple world; phenomena such as form and sound are what are called "marks."

The sensory faculties and their objects are the causes that bind all sentient beings; if one can refrain from craving and attachment toward these marks, all fetters will be eliminated, and one will abide in peace, bliss, and sovereignty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnaśikhin, seated upon an exquisite throne within the great assembly, addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha with these words:

"Venerable One, you are the foremost among the assemblies of bodhisattvas in billions of Buddha-fields; you have attained supreme wisdom and fully realized all knowable phenomena. You have clearly perceived all immeasurable *siddhāntas* and are able to purify the doubts of those in the assembly of yogins."
He thoroughly understands the fundamental origin of the bodies of sentient beings and is able to expound upon them for an eon or more than an eon with exquisite voice and words without weariness.

For what reason does he not explain to you, noble ones, the true Dharma that transcends all causes of opposition and conformity—both apparent and non-apparent—so that those of wisdom may have pure minds free from doubt and, by relinquishing the causal conditions of the aggregates, swiftly attain liberation?
Dharma and non-Dharma are the causes and conditions for the aggregates, giving rise to this body and future bodies.
Wisdom can liberate one from suffering, whereas craving constitutes a firm bond.
Venerable One!

The minds of sentient beings, due to conditions such as form, light, and mental attention, scatter toward objects; these minds are so swift that they are difficult to perceive, and they are turbid and disordered by ignorance, craving, and karma.
"Venerable One!

Among the various phenomena within the bodies of sentient beings, the mind is the precursor, the mind is the swiftest, and the mind is the most preeminent. Whatever phenomena correspond with the mind, those phenomena all take the mind as their essential nature, just as a mani jewel manifests a variety of colors."
Why do you not explain such a meaning?
Furthermore, just as a mani jewel of manifold colors manifests various radiances according to what it encounters, so too are you:

possessing the form of a Tathāgata, dwelling in the Palace of Sovereignty, and surrounded by the assembly of all Buddha-sons, you should likewise preach the Dharma in accordance with what is appropriate.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha said:

"The Land of Buddha-Bliss (Ghanavyūha) is the most serene, it is Great Nirvāṇa, it is wondrous liberation, and it is the Pure Dharma-realm. It is also the dwelling place of those practitioners who cultivate various meditations through wisdom and supernormal powers; it is primordially and eternally abiding, indestructible and imperishable. Water cannot moisten it, and wind cannot dry it. Unlike jars and such things produced by strenuous effort which soon break apart, it is not established by either similar causes or dissimilar causes."
Why is this? Because the thesis (*pakṣa*) and its various members (*avayava*) are indeterminate phenomena, as the various theses and reasons differ from one another.

The *Ghanavyūha* Buddha-field is the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) of consciousness that transcends the discriminating mind; it is not an object within the range of deluded perceptions.

The Ghanavyūha Buddha-field is the abode of the Tathāgatas; it is without beginning and without end. It is not produced from atoms, nor produced from self-nature (*svabhāva*), nor produced from desire; it does not arise from Maheśvara, nor is it produced by ignorance, craving, or karma. Rather, it is brought forth solely by effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), transcending the net of darkness within the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, and the heavens of non-perception.

The *Ghanavyūha* Buddha-field and the *ārya-siddhānta* are not the objective domain to be measured by those who rely on logic (*hetuvidyā*), nor are they revealed by such systems as the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*), the Sovereign Lord (*īśvara*), the Grammarians (*śabdavādin*), or the Vedas; even the power of wisdom at the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) cannot illuminate them. They are exclusively the realm of pure gnosis cultivated by the Tathāgatas across the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
"O virtuous ones!

All ordinary worldlings are deluded regarding what constitutes karma and what does not in this world; I shall now explain the meaning of karma and non-karma, so that those established in meditative concentration may attain peace and happiness."
Then he spoke in verse:
"All things, internal and external, Are seen as nothing but one's own mind;
The dual nature of the minds of sentient beings Consists of the grasper and the grasped."
The essence of mind has two gates; through the mind itself, one perceives all things.
Ordinary beings are deluded in nature and cannot comprehend their own [nature].
All the various realms that are perceived are entirely the products of oneself.
When the appearances of jars and such manifest before one, though sought, they are found to have no essence at all.
The wisdom of the various sages is subtle and inferior;
they cannot know clearly and thus abandon the principle of ultimate reality to travel the path of conceptual discrimination.
This mind has two natures: like a mirror containing myriad images, or like water manifesting the moon;
yet to those with cataracts, it appears as floating hairs.
These floating hairs, necklaces, and pearls—all of these are utterly non-existent.
It is only due to the cataracts of illness in the eye that things appear in this way.
The jar and the cloth are both one's own consciousness; sentient beings are likewise so.
Those who falsely conceptualize and cling do not realize this, yet they constantly grasp at them.
Sentient beings, jars, and the like— these various forms and appearances,
though differing internally and externally, all arise from the mind.
This wondrous samādhi of the Guhyasamāja is not possessed by others.
If there are those who are able to practice, they will be born in lands of manifold merit;
or they will be born among the gods of the desire realm who possess mastery, as well as in the heavens of the form realm,
even up to the palace of the non-percipient beings and the station of Akaniṣṭha.
In the stages of emptiness, consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception—within these various levels—one gradually eliminates craving and desire.
Abiding therein is not the ultimate state; soon one is reborn in the Ghanavyūha.
Surrounded by a host of Buddha-sons, he sports with sovereign ease.
You should cultivate this samādhi; why are you attached to your kin?
Family members bind one another, serving as the cause for wandering through birth and death.
When man and woman are mutually immersed in passion, their vital essence and blood unite;
just as worms are born from foul mud, so too is birth within this [womb].
After nine or ten months, the various sense faculties gradually reach maturity.
When the time arrived, he emerged from his mother’s womb like a wriggling insect;
from that point he grew until his mind attained full understanding.
As I observe all sentient beings, I see that their births and lives are exactly like this.
Parents are beyond counting, and so too are wives and children;
throughout all the worlds, there is nowhere they do not pervade.
It is like a barren woman who, in a dream, suddenly gives birth to a son.
Cradling the joy of the other, he sought him again and saw him lost.
Overwhelmed by grief beyond his own control, he suddenly woke from sleep;
there was no son to be seen, neither at the moment of birth nor at the end.
Furthermore, he dreamed that within mountains and rivers, fields, villages, and cities,
throngs of people were completely filled; they all engaged in various activities together,
seeing one another just as people do in the world.
And upon awakening from sleep, all these are found to be non-existent.
Furthermore, there is a person of great desire who dreams of a woman of exquisite beauty,
her appearance most lovely and her garments and ornaments all rare and splendid.
In a dream one experiences the utmost joy and pleasure, yet upon awakening, nothing is seen;
know that all worldly affairs are exactly like this.
Sovereignty and military forces, parents and other kinsmen—[are likewise empty].
They merely deceive ordinary beings; their essential nature is entirely unreal.
Why do you not diligently cultivate such a concentration?
Immeasurable śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas [rely upon it].
Dwelling in secluded places, where mountain forests are ever tranquil,
or residing by the Ocean of Milk, as well as on Mount Malaya, Sumeru, Vinata, and Mahendra;
From Mount Kailāsa and even the Snowy Mountains,
or at the Kalpavṛkṣa tree, the Pārijāta, beneath the Kuvalaya tree, or atop Mount Bhanduvara, [I have come].
Tasting the flavor of Jambu fruits and various foods of immortality,
Possessing all supernormal powers, they constantly cultivate this contemplation.
Throughout the past and future worlds, they always sit upon lotus flowers.
Sitting with legs crossed, the body unmoving, one constantly observes with right concentration.
The faculties are well-restrained and do not scatter among various objects;
like an elephant caught by a hook, one attains samādhi free from desire.
Whether mundane or supramundane, among all meditative concentrations, the Buddha’s concentration is pure and stainless;
having utterly eliminated all craving and attachment, it prevails within the spheres of totality,
the formless attainments, and the meditations such as the state of non-perception.
One sees the sun, moon, lotuses, The signs of water, fire, and empty space;
If one is free from such conceptual discrimination,
And the mind remains unshaken, Then within samādhi, One beholds immeasurable Buddhas.
At that time, they all extended their hands together, pouring water over his crown.
Thus he entered the stage of Buddhahood; all were clearly awakened, and possessing bodies of manifold forms, he manifested them everywhere according to what was appropriate.
The powers, the superknowledges, the masteries, the samādhis, the dhāraṇīs,
and all such merits— there is none that he has not fully accomplished.
He analyzes all forms, even down to observing the subtlest atoms.
Self-nature is non-existent, like the horns of a tiger or a rabbit;
there is neither part nor possessor of parts. The aggregates and that which possesses aggregates are likewise so;
they are identical to magical illusions, and all things are thus.
Within this, there is no karma and no fruit, nor is there a person who performs action;
there is no agent of the world, for even if one existed, they would not be an agent.
Since an agent depends upon an action, how can one be called an "agent"?
This statement incurs a logical fallacy; the proponent is not pure.
If you ask how it could be so, [consider] the water-circle and the earth-circle, as well as the world of sentient beings, which are all established in successive order.
The various realms of existence each differ; how do they mutually come and go?
Who, moreover, creates the sense faculties that grasp at objects according to their inclinations?
All such things are conceptual constructions, shifting and transforming one after another.
Just as with milk, curd, and butter, so too are arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Whether it be karma or non-karma, people here form false conceptualizations;
those who are steadfast always observe these as being like dreams and the city of the Gandharvas.
Sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been perfumed by conceptual proliferation;
thus they give rise to discrimination and all manner of faults and transgressions.
The sense faculties are like illusions, and their objects are like dreams.
The agent, the act of doing, and the deed— The one established in meditative concentration does not discriminate these.
Those of inferior wisdom give rise to false and evil views,
Imagining the existence of an agent who creates all the world.
Some say it is the mani-jewel, or various ores such as gold and silver;
the diverse colors of birds and beasts, the sharpness and fineness at the tips of thorns—
by whom were these made?
One should know that there is no creator;
the world is not produced by a primal nature (*pradhāna*), nor by causes such as atoms, nor is it without a cause; it does not exist through spontaneous occurrence.
Those whose minds are deluded by false conceptualization do not know its essential nature;
they discriminate whether it is karma or non-karma in this way.
Just as poison enters milk and transforms accordingly, so too does it correspond with its conditions.
So too it is with all phenomena: conceptualization always arises together with them.
The nature of phenomena is neither born nor subject to destruction;
yet those who are deluded fail to understand this, giving rise to various different conceptualizations.
The meditator should observe that the world is merely an accumulation;
whether it be karma or non-karma, one should not dwell upon these thoughts.
Beings come and go among the various realms of existence, just like the sun and the moon.
Abiding in emptiness without support, it moves and turns with the wind.
The nature of karma is extremely subtle and hidden;
those of the Guhyasamāja can perceive it, and thus practitioners of meditative cultivation are not bound by it.
Just as fire consumes wood, turning it to ashes in an instant,
so too should one know that the fire of wisdom burns away the fuel of karma.
Furthermore, just as a lamp dispels darkness, exhausting it entirely in a single thought-moment.
"The darkness of all karmas, accumulated through the熏習 (*vāsanā*) of many kalpas, is entirely extinguished in a single instant when illuminated by the lamp of the Muni’s wisdom.
Chapter Five: Distinguishing the Practice of Contemplation (*Vibhaṅga-caryā-vibhāga-parivarta*). At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha again addressed the great assembly:
“O virtuous ones!

It is like a person in a desolate place who constructs a dwelling by thatching it with mud, tiles, grass, and wood; yet, upon close examination, one finds that within each individual material, no house can be found.”
Furthermore, just as many fingers together form a fist, yet if one seeks the fist apart from the fingers, it is found to be nothing at all;

so too, things such as armies, vehicles, cities, mountains, forests, jars, and garments are all formed through combination. When the wise contemplate them, they see that they are entirely like dream-events.

The body-dwelling of an ordinary person is likewise so: the accumulation of the various elements is like a high mountain, precarious and unstable like a dilapidated house; it is neither born nor extinguished, neither self nor other; like a city of the gandharvas, like a shadow, like a cloud, like a mirage, and like a painted image—though it can be perceived by the senses, its nature is eternally pure, far removed from all conceptualizations of existence and non-existence.

Just as the blind and the lame rely upon one another to travel and thus lack any inherent nature, so too, when analyzed down to the level of subtle atoms, there is nothing but empty names and no substantial reality whatsoever.
If those who are concentrated in meditative absorption engage in such reflection, they will not give rise to discursive thoughts regarding phenomena such as forms and sounds.

Once free from such discursive thoughts, the mind attains rest; they become serenely liberated, no longer undergoing the various states of existence, and constantly delight in the practice of profound meditative concentration.
Celestial immortals and other divine beings, as well as beautiful women, came to make offerings; yet, as if observing a dream, he gave rise to no defiled attachment.
Although his body was present here, none—from the various immortals and non-Buddhist practitioners of incantations up to the Brahma Heaven—could see the crown of his head.
Before long, this person shall be born within the palace of the Maṇi-jewel treasury, sporting with supernormal powers and endowed with all merits.

This dharma of contemplative practice is the sphere of activity for those of great resolve; you, O virtuous one, should swiftly give rise to the vast mind. Those of great resolve quickly attain birth in the Palace of Radiance, free from all greed, hatred, and delusion, and shall eventually proceed to the Ghanavyūha Buddha-field.
This land is vast, subtle, and tranquil; it is free from the afflictions of old age, death, and decline. It is remote from all signs and beyond the range of consciousness.
It cannot be attained by those who rely on false conceptualization.
O virtuous ones!

This land is the dwelling place of those who practice pure contemplation; if you harbor a longing for it, you should diligently cultivate its practices, severing greed, hatred, and delusion, and relinquishing the notions of "I" and "mine."
Why is this? Because the afflictions such as greed seize upon various objects; once an object is seized, the three types of perception arise.

For example, if there is a woman who is beautiful and pleasing, one with much lust, upon seeing her, gives rise to attachment and a mind of desire that becomes deluded and distracted. Whether walking, sitting, eating, drinking, or sleeping, he dwells exclusively on thoughts and reflections of her, having no other thoughts whatsoever.

The physical appearance of that woman constantly manifests within the mind, and this mind is thereby turbid and disturbed by the mire of sensory objects; therefore, one should not harbor greedy attachment toward such objects.
O virtuous ones!
For example, suppose there is a person who, having seen horned animals such as oxen, deer, and goats, develops the notion that tigers and rabbits are without horns.
If he were not to see oxen and others with horns, he would certainly never give rise to the perception that tigers and rabbits lack horns.

The false views of the world are all likewise: they falsely give rise to existence and conceptual discrimination; yet, when one later seeks their essence, it cannot be found. Therefore, they claim that all phenomena are definitively non-existent.
As long as one has not yet abandoned the mind of conceptual discrimination, such unequal perceptions will constantly arise.
O virtuous ones!
You should examine with wisdom and discernment that all objects within the range of the mind's activity are like the false imaginings of seeing a cow or a rabbit.

If these sons of the Buddha contemplate in this manner, according to their aspirations they may be born among humans as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), possessing great majesty and power to travel through the air;

or they may be born in the palaces of the sun, moon, and stars, or in the heavens of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three Gods, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, up to the Maṇi-treasury palace of the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
or they may be born in the Brahma-body and other heavens of the Form Realm, practicing meditative concentration in the ten abodes of the Brahmās.

The Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha), the Heaven of No Heat (Atapa), the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa), the Heaven of Good Appearance (Sudarśana), the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the Sphere of Infinite Space (Ākāśānantyāyatana), the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (Vijñānānantyāyatana), the Sphere of Nothingness (Ākiṃcanyāyatana), and the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
"Abiding therein, one gradually eliminates desire; from this, a pure buddha-field arises, where one constantly dwells in sublime concentration until reaching true liberation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha spoke again in verse:
"Just as when a jar is broken, It becomes shards; Moment by moment they are distinct,"
The permanent is impermanent.
From the seed the sprout arises; when the sprout arises, the seed perishes.
It is like a potter who fashions a jar from clay; the clay is the *śamatha*.
The jar will be of that same color.
If, however, it is made from clay of various colors and fired until matured, then each distinct color will arise within it.
Bamboo shoots grow from onions, and scallions grow from garlic; in impure places, maggots are born from flies.
Within this world, there are fruits that resemble their causes, yet there are also various things that do not resemble their causes;
in all cases, it is through the transformation and decay of the cause that the fruit arises.
Causes such as atoms do not undergo transformation or destruction in their essence; one should not falsely engage in such conceptual discrimination.
There is no creator-self, nor an internal self, a superior self, nor even a mental self, regarding the objects of the sense faculties.
With the coming together of conditions as cause, consciousness arises.
Through skillful means, the wise one thoroughly understands all objects, thereby destroying afflictions and all demons.
In this world there is craving and attachment, like finding honey in a meadow; if craving and attachment are removed, all bonds are completely severed.
Just as a snake bites a creature, so too is the poison of hatred; within the realms of birth and death, it causes much affliction and harm.
"Virtuous ones, if you wish to cause those [defilements] to be completely eliminated, each of you should diligently apply the mind to cultivate the practice of contemplation.

Chapter Six: The Establishment of the Ālaya-vijñāna (Middle Section) The Mahāyāna-śrī-mālā-samādhi Sūtra, Chapter Six: The Establishment of the Ālaya-vijñāna. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha again addressed the assembly, saying:
"Virtuous ones!..."

I recall that in the past, having received the empowerment of the Buddha, I attained a wondrous samādhi; therein, I clearly perceived, with vast clarity, the lands of the ten directions, as well as the abodes of those who cultivate worldly concentrations, and the dwellings of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Within such a realm, the Buddha-land of Ghanavyūha is the foremost in bliss; there, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust dwell within the Lotus Treasury. At that time, I gazed upon them with single-minded devotion.
Emerging from meditative concentration, he immediately saw himself and the various bodhisattvas in the Land of Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha).

At that time, he further beheld the Treasury of Liberation residing within the palace; it was as small in size as a finger joint, its color and appearance bright and pure like an *ātasi* flower, and like the clear, full moon in the sky.
Having seen this at that time, I immediately gave rise to this thought: "Who is this?
For such an inconceivable matter as this has occurred."
As he was thinking this, he immediately saw my body within his own body, and therein he universally beheld all worlds.
At that time, the immeasurable bodhisattvas within the Lotus Treasury, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, also saw in this same way and all conceived this thought:
"This is rare and inconceivable."
At that time, when the Deity among Deities had completed his task, he withdrew his supernormal powers, and all the bodhisattvas returned to their former states.
Having witnessed this rare occurrence, I realized that the various manifestations of the bodhisattvas were the inconceivable realm of the Buddha.
"O virtuous ones!

When the Tathāgata was formerly a bodhisattva, from the first stage, the Joyful, up to the stage of the Cloud of Dharma, he attained inexhaustible dhāraṇīs of words and meanings, as well as the great samādhis such as Śūraṅgama, the eight kinds of mastery of the mind-made body, and manifested according to need the names, radiance, and playful supernatural powers."

Having thus fully accomplished all such merits, they become even more purified, attain perfect enlightenment, and dwell in the Ghanavyūha realm, manifesting transformations according to the needs of beings.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, manifesting in various forms and images, spontaneously pervade all worlds and turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma, causing all sentient beings to swiftly extinguish the darkness of ignorance and practice wholesome dharmas.

There are some bodhisattvas who see the Buddha’s physical marks, such as those of Śrīvaccha and others, fully adorned with natural radiance like a blazing fire; together with other bodhisattvas, they dwell in palaces as pure as lotuses, constantly sporting in sublime samādhi for their peace and bliss.
In some places, they saw the Great Tree Kinnara King manifesting hundreds of billions of various transformations, like the light of the moon pervading all lands.

In others, they saw immeasurable sons of the Buddha, adorned with wisdom and skillful means and graced by manifold marks; wearing jeweled crowns upon their heads and necklaces upon their bodies, they dwelt in the palaces of the Tuṣita Heaven and other celestial realms.

In some instances, they see Samantabhadra possessing great majestic power, having attained omniscience and unimpeded eloquence; his physical form and radiance are peerless and beyond compare, and the palace where he dwells is like the pure, full moon.

Although he dwells within the ocean of the Samādhi of the Secret Adornment, he manifests all manner of forms and images, pervading everywhere; he is praised by all the worthy and holy ones, and is surrounded and guarded by immeasurable devas, gandharvas, and others, as well as kings, princes, and their retinues.

Or again, one may see a master of contemplative practice surrounded by a multitude of Buddha-sons, dwelling in the tranquility of dhyāna as if in sleep, yet free from the faults of torpor and indolence, having served immeasurable Buddhas in the past.

Furthermore, some see him as the Great Teacher, manifesting his descent into a womb, birth, renunciation, ascetic practice, single-minded right concentration, and even parinirvāṇa; performing various miraculous transformations while walking, standing, sitting, or reclining in mid-air, such that all devas and humans from Jambudvīpa up to Akaniṣṭha heaven cannot fail to gaze upon him in reverence.
"O virtuous ones!
The essential nature of all Buddhas is known only by the Buddhas themselves; the wisdom of the Buddhas is supreme and peerless.
Just as Śākyamuni, the lion among men, has already attained it, so shall you, all sons of the Buddha, likewise attain it."
Therefore, you virtuous ones should give rise to pure faith;

believing that the Buddha-nature will surely lead to liberation, such persons may become universal monarchs (cakravartin) or various minor kings, or even be born in the palaces of the Brahma heavens as lords of gods.

These sons of the Buddha further increase their diligence; in the pure buddha-field of the Lotus Treasury, they are born by lotus-transformation together with other bodhisattvas, enter the path of the One Vehicle, abandon the habits of greed and other afflictions, and even subdue the celestial Māras of the desire realm.
Now, as for diligence, its resolve is free from cowardice; it causes the Buddha-family to flourish and reigns supreme over all lands.
O virtuous ones!

If you wish to become a Buddha, you must purify the Buddha-lineage. Once the lineage is purified, you will surely receive a prediction of enlightenment from a Tathāgata and bring benefit to all practitioners.

For example, it is like the great earth, which serves as the support for all sentient beings; or like a skilled physician who skillfully compiles various medicines and travels through cities and towns to provide universal healing with a compassionate heart.

The Buddha is also like this: his mind is impartial in teaching and transforming others and remains free from discrimination; even if sentient beings were to cut and slice his flesh and skin, his mind would remain unmoved.
O virtuous ones!
The internal and external objects that constitute the range of the mind are all merely consciousness, appearing through delusion; herein there is neither self nor what belongs to a self.

The harmer, the harmed, the act of harming, and the instruments of harm—all these are the objective domain of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which discriminates in this manner based upon the *ālayavijñāna*.
For example, suppose a person places a jewel in the sun, and by means of a fire-drill, fire is produced; this fire is not born from the jewel nor from the fire-drill, nor is it created by the person.

The mind, intellect, and consciousness are likewise thus: they arise from the conjunction of the sense faculties, objects, and mental attention. This nature is not like the deceptive perceptions of a mirage, a dream, or an illusion; nor is it like the hair of a tortoise or a frog, or the horns of a rabbit.
Is the fire of a thunderclap produced from water, produced from lightning, or produced from the thunder?
No one can definitively know its source.
Just as one sees a potter fashioning a jar and so forth, it is likewise with mental factors such as desire, which arise simultaneously with the mind.
O virtuous ones!
The essential nature of the mind is inconceivable; those who dwell in Ghanavyūha are well able to know and perceive it.
O virtuous ones!
The ālayavijñāna of all sentient beings has existed from the beginning; it is perfectly pure, transcends the world, and is identical to nirvāṇa.
It is like the bright moon appearing in all lands: though people of the world see it as waning and waxing, the essential nature of the moon never increases or decreases.

The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is likewise: it manifests universally within the realms of all sentient beings, its nature eternally perfect and pure, neither increasing nor decreasing; yet those without wisdom give rise to false conceptual attachments.

If there are those who can correctly understand this, they will immediately attain the distinction of the untainted transformation of the basis (*anāsrava-āśraya-parāvṛtti*). This distinct dharma is extremely difficult to attain;
it is like the moon, which by its very nature remains eternally bright and pure even when within the clouds.

The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is likewise: it remains eternally pure amidst the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) within the objective spheres of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
It is like a piece of wood in a river that drifts along with the current; yet the wood and the current are distinct in their respective natures.
The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is likewise: although the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the various consciousnesses are constantly present with it, they do not contaminate it.

O virtuous ones! The *ālayavijñāna* serves as the support for all phenomena, both defiled and pure; it is the object of the samādhi of "abiding in happiness in the present life" for the noble ones; it is the cause for all realms of existence, such as those of humans and devas, as well as for all Buddha-lands; and it constantly serves as the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) for all vehicles (*yāna*). If one can realize this, one immediately attains the path of Buddhahood.
"O virtuous ones!

All sentient beings possess the power and sovereignty of accumulated merit, even when born in places of peril and hardship; the ālayavijñāna constantly dwells within them, serving as their fundamental support."

This is the realm of sentient beings from beginningless time; the habitual tendencies of various karmas can increase themselves and can also increase the other seven consciousnesses. Because of this, ordinary people grasp at it as an internal self that acts and is acted upon.
O virtuous ones!
The mind resides within the body, revolving as swiftly as the wind; stirred by the winds of karma, it pervades all the sense faculties, and the seven consciousnesses arise simultaneously like waves.
The *pradhāna* (primordial nature), atoms, Īśvara, time, and so forth, which are postulated by the non-Buddhists, are all in fact the pure ālayavijñāna. O worthy ones!
The ālayavijñāna, with the power of prior karma and craving as its causes, brings about the various categories of the world; yet those who engage in false conceptualization grasp it as a creator.

"The essence and characteristics of this consciousness are subtle and difficult to know; failing to perceive the reality, the mind becomes deluded and fails to understand, thereby giving rise to craving and attachment toward the faculties, objects, and mentation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha spoke again in verse:
"You sons of the Buddhas, why do you not see or hear [this]?"
The essence of the ālayavijñāna is pure, the support for all bodies;
it manifests as the thirty-two marks of a Buddha or as a universal monarch,
or takes on various forms, which all in the world behold.
Just as the pure moon in the sky is surrounded by a multitude of stars,
so do the various consciousnesses abide within the body of the ālayavijñāna.
Just as the Lord of the Desire Realm wanders through his jewel palace attended by his retinue, [so does the ālaya dwell within the body].
Just as the various deities of rivers and seas exercise mastery within the waters,
so too should one know that the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) abides in the world;
just as the earth gives rise to all things, this mind manifests in manifold ways.
Just as the Sun Deity, resplendent, rides his precious palace,
Circumambulates Mount Sumeru, and flows everywhere to illuminate the world below,
So that all the devas and the people of the world, upon seeing him, pay him homage and respect.
Within the Buddha-ground of the ālayavijñāna, its characteristics are likewise so;
practicing the various deeds of the ten stages, it manifests the Mahāyāna Dharma,
universally bestowing happiness upon sentient beings, and constantly praising the Tathāgata.
Residing within the body of a bodhisattva, this is precisely what is called a "bodhisattva.
Both the Buddha and all bodhisattvas are designated by the name Ālaya.
The Buddha and all his spiritual heirs—those who have already received or shall receive the prediction of enlightenment—are likewise so named.
The vast ālaya-vijñāna becomes perfect awakening;
The practitioners of the Guhyasamāja, endowed with sublime samādhi,
Are able to clearly perceive and observe the ālaya.
The Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and those of other paths—
those who perceive the principle without fear— all observe this very consciousness.
The various objects of the diverse consciousnesses are all transformations of the mind.
Objects such as jars and garments—such natures do not exist at all;
they all depend upon the ālayavijñāna. Sentient beings perceive them through delusion, and due to various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the grasped and the grasper revolve.
This nature is not like an illusion, a mirage, or the optical illusion of falling hairs;
it is neither produced nor unproduced, neither empty nor existent.
Just as with the relationship between long and short, when one is absent, all are non-existent.
The wise observe illusory phenomena and see that these are all merely magical illusions;
never has there been a single thing that arises simultaneously with the illusion.
Like a mirage or the optical illusion of falling hairs, they are perceived through the conjunction of conditions.
Apart from one, there is no combination; the past and future likewise do not exist.
Illusions, hair-nets, and so forth—all these various phenomenal characteristics are transformations of the mind; they have no substance and no names.
People deluded within the world, their minds lacking self-mastery,
falsely claim that there is a magician who creates various objects through illusion.
Yet the magician’s bricks, tiles, and other such materials— whatever various things he produces— [are likewise empty].
Movement and turning, such as coming and going— these perceptions are all unreal.
Just as iron shifts and turns toward a magnet, so too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna),
which evolves in accordance with conceptual discrimination.
Throughout all worlds, there is nowhere it does not pervade.
Like the sun or a mani-jewel, it is without thought or discrimination;
this consciousness pervades all places, and its manifestation is called transmigration.
Neither dying nor being born, it is fundamentally not a phenomenon of saṃsāra.
When the practitioner observes with diligence that birth and death are like a dream,
at that moment there is the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), which is called liberation.
This is the supreme teaching and principle of all Buddhas,
which scrutinizes all phenomena like a scale, like a clear mirror,
like a great bright lamp, and also like a touchstone.
Far removed from annihilation, it is the hallmark of the Noble Path.
For those who practice sublime meditative concentration, it is the cause for reaching liberation;
forever free from all defilements, it manifests through the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
The Mahāyāna-Guhyaka-Śrī-mālā Sūtra, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Divākara of India during the Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Seven: The Sphere of the Eye-Consciousness (Part Two).

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha surveyed the ten directions and emitted a great radiance from the jewel within his topknot. This light shone universally upon all lands and the assembly of Bodhisattvas within the Ghanavyūha.
Having emitted this light, he immediately addressed the Bodhisattva Yathārthadarśin, saying:
"O Lord! Within the Snowy Mountains there is a malevolent beast named 'The Harmer,' who employs hundreds of thousands of deceptions to capture various beasts, killing and eating them."
If they see a female deer that has fawns, they will call out to her with a mournful cry like the sound of a fawn.
If they see a male deer, they will manifest horns to resemble him and approach him with intimacy; thus, the deer feel no alarm or fear, and [the practitioners] kill and eat them.
Just as one sees various beasts such as oxen and horses, all assuming those very forms to indulge in their wickedness;

so too, O Benevolent Lord, is it with the view of self produced by all non-Buddhists regarding the *ālayavijñāna*. Like those evil beasts transforming into various shapes, the characteristics of the self grasped by those attached to a self differ from one another, even down to the smallest, like a mote of dust.
O Benevolent Lord!
Upon what do these various forms of self-grasping abide?
They do not abide elsewhere, but abide solely within one's own consciousness.
Those who maintain the view of a self say:
"The self, the mental faculty, and the object come together.
It is through the conjunction of the mind and so forth that consciousness arises; fundamentally, there is no self.
Just as cloth and flowers, when combined, possess fragrance, yet no fragrance can be perceived when they are not combined;

therefore, one should know that there is only consciousness—the mind and its mental factors—and no separate self (ātman) that can be apprehended, such as a fruit within a bowl, a lamp within a cage, or the *iṣikā-viśa* grass.

It is only through causes and conditions that mind and mental factors arise; herein there is no self and no arising. This subtle, single characteristic is primordially quiescent; it is the realm of internal realization for those who practice the contemplative path of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The various non-Buddhists, failing to understand that it is consciousness-only that gives rise to the view of a self, lack the wisdom regarding phenomena and thus forcibly engage in conceptual discrimination, clinging to existence or non-existence, and to arguments concerning a self and what belongs to a self—whether as one or as many—just as those wicked beasts cause much injury and slaughter.

It is just like this: it causes all sentient beings to rush back and forth within birth and death, refusing to draw near to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). As they wander further and further away without a place of refuge, they turn their backs on the Noble Path and lose their own benefit. Within the three vehicles, they do not even attain the Dharma of the Single Vehicle; bound by grasping, they do not perceive the True Reality (tattva) and cannot enter the land of Ghanavyūha, nor can they even hear its name.
"O Benevolent Lord!

All practitioners of contemplation purify the view of self within this very consciousness; you and all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should likewise do so—diligently practicing it yourselves and explaining it to others, so that they may swiftly enter the Buddha-land of Ghanavyūha."

Chapter 8: The Subtle and Secret Nature of the Ālaya (Part II) The Mahāyāna-śrī-mālā-sūtra, Chapter Eight: The Subtle and Secret Nature of the Ālaya At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Ratnapāṇi, who addressed King Varaprabhāsvara:

"Your Majesty should question Vajragarbha, who abides in samādhi, regarding all phenomena existing in the world: apart from all conceptualization and names—whether names that are non-corresponding or names that are corresponding—in what does the intrinsic nature of those phenomena abide?"
"O sons of the Buddha, listen with single-minded resolve.
Then King Saṃdarśanasuvikrānta questioned him in accordance with that meaning, saying:
"The realms of names and conceptions, and all worldly phenomena—"
Is it merely conceptual construction, or does it exist apart from conceptual construction?
Regarding the names as they are established, where do these names abide?
O Vajra-Svāmin, I pray that you explain this for me.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha replied in verse:
"The various phenomena of the world Are all nothing but names;
Established merely by conceptualization, Apart from the name, there is no separate referent."
The four aggregates are merely names; therefore, they are called "name" (*nāman*).
Just as one says "Māṇava," there is only the name and no substantial entity.
The Buddha and his sons of the Buddha teach that name exists only in its marks (*nimitta*).
Names exist apart from characteristics; one should not make such discriminations.
Therefore, based upon characteristics, one discriminates various names;
like the word "ghee" (*ghṛta*) and so forth, these all lack any reality.
Whatever is conceptually constructed by ordinary beings all relies upon signs;
therefore, worldly phenomena are entirely non-existent apart from their signs.
Vases, garments, vehicles, and the like are merely what are conceptually constructed through names and expressions.
Although the characteristics of form can be described, its essential nature does not exist.
All worldly phenomena of form consist of nothing but these characteristics;
names are established based solely upon these characteristics, and thus they are called "things without reality."
The King should contemplate the nature of worldly phenomena: apart from names, nothing exists;
it is only through the discriminating mind that grasping and attachment arise.
If one is free from discrimination, grasping and attachment will not arise.
Non-arising is itself the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), through which one realizes the inexhaustible Dharma.
Therefore, O Great Kings and others, you should constantly contemplate that all things are merely the discriminating mind; apart from this, nothing exists.
The growth of form, characteristics, and substance; the dispersal and destruction of matter and the body—these and other such various names are all merely conceptualizations of form (*rūpa*).
Conceptualization, names, and discrimination are fundamentally no different in their essential nature.
In accordance with conventional meaning, they are established as different.
If one abandons names and seeks the substantial entity,
then in both the past and the future, nothing at all can be found.
One can know the arising of all consciousnesses, yet there is no dharma that is known;
what is known is merely a name, and all worldly phenomena are thus.
One discriminates dharmas by means of names, but dharmas do not correspond to their names.
The nature of all phenomena is thus: it does not abide in conceptual discrimination.
Because phenomena are merely names, perception has no intrinsic substance;
since perception is absent, names are likewise non-existent. Where, then, could conceptual discrimination exist?
If one attains non-conceptuality, body and mind are eternally tranquil;
like wood that has been consumed by fire, it will ultimately never arise again.
It is like a person carrying a burden; such a person is called a "burden-bearer."
According to the differences in what is carried, there are distinctions among those who carry;
the name is like the object carried, and one distinguishes the carrier by the name.
Because names are manifold, these distinctions are each different.
As when one sees a stump as a person, or sees a person as a stump—
the dual discrimination between "person" and "stump" exists only as a name.
Within the combination of the great elements, one discriminates them as "form."
If one is separated from the great elements, the nature of form does not exist.
Just as qualities depend on a jar, so too does the jar depend on its name;
if one sets aside the name to seek the jar, the jar can ultimately never be found.
A jar does not abide in the essence of a jar; how could a name abide in a name?
Since conceptualization arises from the conjunction of these two, even the measure of names does not exist.
Abiding in such meditative concentration, one’s mind remains unshakable.
For example, just as gold, stone, and the like, though originally devoid of the nature of water, flow like water when combined with fire;
so too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna): its essence is not a phenomenon subject to transmigration.
The various consciousnesses are associated together, Flowing along in tandem with mental factors (*dharma*).
Just as iron moves in a circle because of a magnet,
Both are devoid of volition, yet they appear as if possessing thought and awareness.
The ālayavijñāna and the seven consciousnesses should be known to be likewise.
Bound by the ropes of habitual tendencies, though there is no person, it appears as if there were;
pervading the bodies of all sentient beings, it wanders through all perilous realms of existence.
Like iron and the magnet, they do not know one another through their mutual interaction.
Having departed from perilous paths, they come to dwell in the various stages;
with the sovereign power of spiritual penetrations, they are like the illusory Śūraṅgama.
Even up to the dhāraṇīs, there is nothing that is not fully accomplished.
Praising the Buddha’s true merits serves as an offering;
sometimes he manifests immeasurable bodies, or a single body with immeasurable hands.
From their shoulders, mouths, and tongues, they emanate infinite successions of bodies;
they travel to the lands of the ten directions to make offerings to all Tathāgatas,
raining down various exquisite flowers, precious robes, and necklaces.
These accumulations were exceedingly high and vast, like Mount Sumeru and other mountains;
with them they made offerings to the Tathāgatas and all the Bodhisattvas.
Some constructed precious palaces, like clouds arrayed in myriad colors.
They manifest as celestial maidens, dwelling and sporting therein;
with the wondrous sounds of music and song, they make offerings to all Buddhas.
Or they always remain together with Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, traveling and staying side by side.
All the hosts of Māras and enemies he subdues with sovereign ease.
Having attained self-realized samādhi and already transformed the basis of existence, he proclaims the fivefold dharma: the eight consciousnesses and selflessness.
The succession [of manifestations] never pauses for a moment; with single-minded devotion, one makes offerings.
Sometimes he manifests a small body, its size like a mote of dust;
again he manifests a great body, boundless and unfathomable.
With all manner of diverse forms and appearances, they make offerings to the Tathāgata.
Or, within their own bodies, they universally contain all worlds;
furthermore, they place all those worlds inside a single mustard seed.
The great ocean becomes a cow’s footprint, and the cow’s footprint likewise becomes the ocean;
yet the sentient beings therein experience no disturbance of body or mind.
All necessities for life are provided equally, bringing benefit to all.
Like the sun and moon, like the earth, Like water, fire, and wind, and also like a great island of jewels, And like excellent, wondrous medicine.
All phenomena are neither born nor extinguished; Neither interrupted nor eternal.
Unity and difference, as well as coming and going—none of these exist at all.
To falsely establish various names is the nature of parikalpita (the imagined).
All phenomena are like illusions, like dreams, and like cities of the gandharvas.
A mirage, the moon in water, a whirling firebrand, clouds, lightning, and the like—
what is falsely grasped therein is the nature of universal imagination (parikalpita-svabhāva).
Various names are used to describe various phenomena.
All these are non-existent; this is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
All phenomena of the world do not transcend name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*);
these all possess only names, and apart from names there is no separate referent.
Such is the nature of pervasive conceptualization; I call this the world.
With the eye, forms, and so forth as conditions, the threefold conjunction arises;
sound issues from the drumstick and the drum, and the sprout grows from the earth and the seed.
The palace, the jar, and the garment—none of these arise except through a multitude of conditions.
Sentient beings and all phenomena are likewise entirely of the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
If a phenomenon is untainted (*anāsrava*), its meaning cannot be abandoned.
The source from which realized wisdom arises—this nature is called the reality.
The various distinctions among the characteristics of all phenomena have already been explained as their intrinsic nature;
if one were to depart from this gateway of intrinsic nature, all phenomena would not be clearly understood.
Just as a person uses various materials to magically create diverse forms, though their colors and appearances differ, their nature is in all cases indeterminate.
All worldly affairs are exactly like this; the various things are none of them real.
That which is grasped by deluded sentiments is entirely the product of pervasive conceptualization.
Just as a mani jewel manifests images according to the colors [of objects], so too is it with the world:
it exists only in accordance with one's discrimination.
The essence and its function have no location; this is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Like a city of the gandharvas, it is not a city yet appears as one;
nor is it without a cause that allows it to manifest in such a way.
All the various things in the world should be known to be likewise:
the sun, the moon, the mountains, houses, smoke, clouds, and so forth—
though their essential forms differ from one another, they have never been confused or intermingled.
Arising from self, from another, or from both, their essential nature is entirely unestablished;
they are merely what is conceptualized, the nature of pervasive imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
All things do not arise from causes, nor are they without cause.
Whether existent or non-existent, these are all attachments of the mind.
Names arise based on signs; both [existence and non-existence] are born from conceptual construction.
Right knowledge and suchness are far removed from conceptual construction.
The mind appears as manifestations, and these manifestations are the support for the intellect (*manas*).
The intellect and the five sense-minds arise together, just like waves upon the ocean.
Habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have no beginning, and the same is true for objective spheres (*viṣaya*).
The mind arises from habitual tendencies, and objects cause the mind to be deluded.
Relying upon the ālayavijñāna, all seeds exist;
when the mind appears as objects, this is called the world.
The seven consciousnesses and the ālayavijñāna arise through the power of mutual conditioning.
These eight kinds of consciousness are neither eternal nor annihilated;
all worlds appear as if they exist, yet are thus arrayed.
Some reckon that for all sentient beings, the triad of self, sense-faculties,
and objects combine to produce various consciousnesses that discern their respective domains.
Others falsely speculate, saying that because of the causes of the agent and karma, [consciousness arises].
Born in the Brahma heavens and so forth, within and without all worlds—
these worlds are not created by a creator, nor by karma or atoms; rather,
it is only the ālayavijñāna that manifests, appearing as if it were external objects.
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is not produced by conditions, nor does the storehouse itself act as a condition;
though the various consciousnesses flow on, there is no triadic conjunction (trikasamnipāta).
The essence of the ālaya is eternally abiding, and the manifold consciousnesses coexist with it.
Like a wheel and a crystal, or like stars together with the moon,
from this arise habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that grow ever anew;
they further increase other consciousnesses, and those other consciousnesses do likewise.
Thus it revolves constantly; only when one awakens does the mind finally rest.
It is like fire burning wood: it shifts and moves gradually;
once this wood is consumed, it proceeds to burn other wood.
Relying upon the ālayavijñāna, the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) likewise gradually eliminates all tainted states (*sāsrava*), forever bringing the phenomena of saṃsāra to rest.
This is the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha*), the realm of samādhi.
The multitude of sages, by means of this path, universally proceed to the lands of the ten directions.
Just as gold within ore cannot be seen,
yet when the wise skillfully smelt and refine it, that gold becomes manifest and clear.

The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is likewise: entangled by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is only after they have been purified through meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that the practitioner of concentration sees it clearly and constantly.
Just as butter can never be obtained from curd if it has not been churned and stirred, [so too cannot the true nature be seen without purification].
Therefore, as the wise churn curd to obtain butter,
so too is it with the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna): though enveloped and obscured by the various consciousnesses,
those in the Śrī-māyā-saṃghāṭa who practice meditative concentration can attain it through diligent contemplation.
The Ghanavyūha is the Great Illumination, a sublime designation for wondrous wisdom;
If sons of the Buddha practice it with diligence, they shall be born in this land.
Whether in the realm of form or the formless realm, In the spheres of emptiness, consciousness, or neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
Having constantly and diligently practiced therein, they have come to be born in this place.
Here, these sons of the Buddha, whose majestic radiance is like that of the sun and moon,
abide on the stages of cultivation and proclaim the principles of correspondence.
The Dharma realized by the Tathāgata, through which one transforms the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) according to what is perceived—
by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, he is conferred empowerment and granted his station.
Although he dwells in the land of Ghanavyūha, he manifests in accordance with the needs of beings as is appropriate.
"Manifesting through transformation within emptiness, as if seeing or hearing the Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha again addressed the great assembly: "O noble ones!"

The ālayavijñāna, from beginningless time, has been bound by the various karmas perfumed by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), resulting in an unceasing cycle of saṃsāra; like an ocean stirred by the wind that gives rise to waves of the various consciousnesses, it is constantly arising and constantly ceasing, neither discontinuous nor eternal.
Yet sentient beings do not realize this themselves; they follow their own consciousness as various objective realms manifest.

If they were to understand this for themselves—as fire consumes fuel—then all [delusions] would be extinguished, and they would enter the stage of outflowlessness (anāsrava), becoming what is called a sage (ārya).
O virtuous ones!

The ālayavijñāna transforms and manifests as various objects, pervading the world; the defiled manas grasps at them through objective conditions, clinging to "I" and "mine"; and the various consciousnesses each discern their respective objects.
"O virtuous ones!
The mind accumulates karma, and the mental faculty (*manas*) is likewise.

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cognizes various phenomena, while the five sensory consciousnesses discriminate the objects present before them. It is like one with cataracts seeing what appears to be a mass of hairs; within a mind that resembles form, they perceive form where there is no form."
"O virtuous ones!
Just as the nature of a maṇi jewel is pure, if it is placed within the light of the sun or moon, it will rain down various things according to what is required."

The ālayavijñāna is likewise thus: it is the pure treasury of all Tathāgatas, which, conjoined with habitual tendencies (vāsanā), transforms to resemble various forms pervading the world; yet when associated with the outflow-free (anāsrava), it rains down all dharmas of merit, just as milk transforms into curd, and from curd into whey.

The ālayavijñāna is likewise: it transforms and manifests as all the various forms of the world, just as one with cataracts, due to the disease of the visual impairment, perceives what appear to be floating hairs.

All sentient beings are likewise: due to the cataracts of habitual tendencies abiding in the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), eyes perceive various semblances of forms; these perceived forms are like a mirage, devoid of both existence and non-existence, and are all manifestations produced by the *ālaya*.
"O virtuous ones!

Based upon the eye and forms, there arises a consciousness of form that resembles form; it is born like a magical illusion and dwells within the eye, its appearance flickering like a mirage in the heat."
O virtuous ones!

All various forms are merely transformations of the ālayavijñāna in conjunction with the habitual tendencies of form, appearing as their semblances; they do not possess a separate substance as is falsely discriminated by the ignorant.
O virtuous ones!
Whether all sentient beings are sitting or lying down, walking or standing, or whether they are in a state of stupor, sleep, or even running about wildly, there is none that is not the ālayavijñāna.
For example, when the midday sun radiates its light upon the earth, the rising vapors shimmer and undulate like flowing water; thirsty animals, deluded, rush toward them.
The ālayavijñāna is likewise: its essential nature is not form, yet it appears as if it were form, leading those who engage in conceptual discrimination to give rise to false grasping and attachment.
Just as the power of a magnet causes iron to move, appearing to possess consciousness though it is actually devoid of consciousness, so too is the ālaya-vijñāna:
sustained by the phenomena of birth and death, it wanders through the various realms of existence, appearing to be a self though it is not a self.
Just as an object within water, though lacking thought or perception, moves along with the flow of the water and does not remain still, so too is the ālayavijñāna:
although it lacks discrimination, it functions in dependence upon the body.
Just as when two elephants contend in a struggle for strength, if one is wounded and retreats without returning, it should be known that the ālayavijñāna is likewise:
once its defiled portions are severed, it no longer undergoes transmigration.
For example, just as a lotus flower emerges from the mud, bright, pure, and free from all dust and defilements, such that gods and noble persons behold it with reverence and esteem;
so too is the ālayavijñāna: having emerged from the mire of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it attains clarity and purity, and is thus held in high regard by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and great beings.
Suppose there were a wondrous jewel, rare and beyond compare in the world, which, when in the hands of a foolish and lowly person, was constantly defiled and held in contempt;
yet when a wise person obtained it, he presented it to the king to adorn his crown for the king to wear.

The ālayavijñāna is likewise so: it is the pure lineage (*gotra*) of all Tathāgatas, which, while in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), is constantly defiled; once realized by Bodhisattvas, they sever all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and it remains perpetually cherished until the attainment of Buddhahood.
Just as a beautiful gem submerged in water is covered by algae, so too is the ālayavijñāna;
