within the ocean of birth and death, it is concealed by various evil habitual tendencies and does not manifest.
O virtuous ones!

The ālayavijñāna manifests in two modes of appearance: the grasper and the grasped. Just as a snake with two heads goes wherever it pleases, so too does this [consciousness] arise together with the appearance of form; worldly people grasp it as form, or they conceive of it as "I" or "mine," as existent or non-existent, acting as the creator of the world and sovereign over the world.
"O virtuous ones!
Although the ālayavijñāna manifests in various ways, its nature is profoundly deep; those without wisdom cannot perceive it.
It is like a magician who conjures various beasts, some walking and some running; though they resemble sentient beings, they possess no fixed reality."
The ālayavijñāna is likewise; it conjures forth the various beings of the world as an illusion, yet there is no substantial reality therein.

Ordinary, deluded people fail to understand this and give rise to false attachments, conceiving views such as those of atoms, pradhāna (the primal nature), Īśvara (the Lord), puruṣa (the person), existence, non-existence, and so forth.
"O virtuous ones!

The mind is able to differentiate all worlds; this differentiated view is like a form within a painting, like a shape within clouds, like objects seen by one afflicted by cataracts or in a dream, like Indra’s bow (a rainbow), like a city of the gandharvas, like an echo, like water in a mirage, like trees reflected in a river, and like the moon’s image in a pond. It is thus that the person who differentiates falsely grasps at the ālayavijñāna."
If there are those who can correctly observe this and know that all worlds are merely one's own mind, then all such conceptualized views will be transformed and extinguished. O noble ones!
The ālayavijñāna is the basis for the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the mind and its various phenomena, and it is turbid due to being disturbed by the discriminating mind.
If one is free from discrimination, it becomes untainted (*anāsrava*); that which is untainted is eternal, just like space.

If Bodhisattvas attain samādhi regarding the ālayavijñāna, they give rise to such meritorious dharmas as untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*), and sovereign supernormal powers (*vaśitā-abhijñā*). Possessing the body born of the ten ultimate vows, they transform their basis within the realm of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*) so that it abides eternally, equal in nature to space—indestructible and inexhaustible.
"O virtuous ones!
The Tathāgata perceives that all worlds are without increase or decrease; one who enters parinirvāṇa is not destroyed, nor is there any non-sentient being who has only now been born."

The lands of the ten directions share the same single dharma-nature; whether the Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, all dharmas abide in the dharma-nature, being neither eternal nor subject to annihilation.

If liberation were the cessation of the realm of sentient beings, it would destroy the omniscient nature of the Tathāgata, and the dharmas known by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present could not be equal.
Furthermore, if nirvana were the extinction of sentient beings, who would be liberated from suffering?
Such claims as the existence of *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* [nirvana], or the subduing of Māra, are all false teachings.

Therefore, one should know that for those practitioners who realize liberation, their bodies abide eternally; they are free from the various aggregates of existence and have extinguished all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
It is like throwing red-hot iron into cold water: although the heat is removed, the iron is not destroyed.
It is just so, O virtuous ones!

Struck by the heavy residues of conceptual proliferation, the ocean of the ālaya gives rise to a continuous succession of waves—the five dharmas, the three natures, and the various consciousnesses. All objective spheres appear with shifting characteristics, manifesting as objects within a realm that is devoid of objective reality.
O virtuous ones!

The ālayavijñāna functions within the dense forest of the aggregates with the manas as its precursor; the manovijñāna discerns various objects such as forms, while the five sensory consciousnesses perceive present objects based on their respective faculties. There is no perceived object that is not, in fact, the ālayavijñāna.

O noble ones! The ālayavijñāna abides in conjunction with life-force, warmth, and touch; the manas abides therein, and consciousness in turn abides in the manas, while the remaining five consciousnesses likewise abide in their respective sense bases.
"O virtuous ones!

Mind, mentation, and consciousness dwell within the aggregates, driven by karma and wandering in transmigration without ceasing. All karmic actions arise from craving; through karma one receives a body, and with that body one again creates karma. Having abandoned this body, one receives another body, moving like a centipede."
The mind and mental factors arise within the various realms of existence, further accumulating the dense forest of aggregates. O noble ones!
If life-force, warmth, and consciousness abandon the body, the body becomes devoid of sensation, like wood or stone.
"O virtuous ones!
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the mind (citta); that which clings to a self is called the intellect (manas); and that which grasps various objects is termed consciousness (vijñāna).
O virtuous ones!"

The mind (*citta*) is able to sustain the body, while the intellect (*manas*) is attached to the various realms of existence; the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) universally discerns the five manifest objects. O virtuous ones!

The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) acts as the cause for the arising of the various consciousnesses; the intellect and the mental consciousness arise immediately following their respective objects of perception (*ālambana*); and the five sensory consciousnesses arise further depending on dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), because they take their simultaneous, respective sense organs as those dominant conditions.
"O virtuous ones!

The body is like a reanimated corpse and like a mirage; it revolves according to the causes and conditions of the various formations (*saṃskāra*). It is neither false nor real; dragged by craving, its nature is empty and without self."
O virtuous ones!

The mental consciousnesses arise together with the mind; furthermore, the five sensory consciousnesses arise simultaneously with the mental consciousness. In this manner, they always function in conjunction with the universal ground (mahābhūmika).
"O virtuous ones!

The ālayavijñāna is perfumed by craving and thereby increases; having increased itself, it further increases the other consciousnesses like an uninterrupted wheel. Because of these various consciousnesses, the various realms of existence arise, and within those realms, consciousness increases once more. Thus, consciousness and the world act as mutual causes for one another."

Just as the current of a river flows on without interruption from beginning to end, and just as sprouts arise in succession from seeds, each distinct and clearly manifest, so too is the movement of consciousness:
having conjoined with the triad [of sense organ, object, and consciousness], it conjoins again, arising in differentiation without cessation, whereby all internal and external phenomena arise.
"All ordinary beings do not understand their own minds; you, sons of the Buddha, should diligently observe this.
At that time, King Most Victorious of All Colors and the others again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Treasury of the Vajra Samādhi, you who have attained fearlessness..."
Skillfully entering the Secret Adorned Realm, they are able to expound all dharmas.
The Buddhas and their spiritual sons, through samādhi and right reflection,
perceive the characteristics of all dharmas as subtle, wondrous, and most peerless.
We pray that the Great Wise One will proclaim for our sake: how you,
O Venerable One, always abide in the palace of the Maṇi Moon-Treasury,
seated upon the lion throne, surrounded by the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
I pray that for the sake of all yogins, you will expound the dharma of the Samādhi of Ghanavyūha;
this is the teaching proclaimed by the Buddha Candradhvaja for the assembly.
That assembly shall come here; I pray that you will speak without weariness.

At that time, the World-Honored One Candradhvaja, with his immeasurable transformation bodies residing in the palaces of the various heavens of the desire and form realms, was surrounded and honored by countless bodhisattvas and devas as he expounded the Dharma of the true mark—the meditative practices cultivated by those who are fearless within the Ghanavyūha.

When those bodhisattvas had heard this teaching, they attained a samādhi corresponding to the wisdom of internal realization; their minds took no pleasure in the bliss of the fixed position (*samyaktva-niyāma*) nor did they abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). While in that state of concentration, they observed one another and each thought to themselves:
"Who among us has already realized the foremost practice of contemplating the true nature of phenomena?"
"How may we come to see such a person?
With hearts filled with longing and reverence, they all remained standing there.
Those sons of the Buddha then reflected once more:
"What is concentration? What is not concentration?
In what is one concentrated, and what are the conditions upon which that concentration depends?"
Having formed this thought, by the power of samādhi he beheld the king of bodhisattvas within the land of Ghanavyūha, wearing a jeweled crown and adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.

Those bodhisattvas then arose from their meditative absorption, donned exquisite robes, and having come to this assembly from immeasurable buddha-fields in other directions, gazed with single-minded devotion upon the Honored One Vajragarbha.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha looked around in the four directions; seeing the great assembly, he gave rise to the thought of wishing to preach the Dharma. With a joyful smile, he uttered a harmonious and elegant voice, and spoke these verses:
“You sons of the Buddhas, All should listen with a single mind.
The state of meditative concentration is difficult to conceive; It is not something realized through discursive thought.”
Concentration and the one who concentrates, as well as the object of concentration, are likewise thus.
Free from all sensual desires and unwholesome states, yet possessing directed thought and evaluation,
with tranquility giving rise to joy and bliss— this is called entering the first dhyāna.
In this manner, proceeding gradually through the four, eight, and up to ten stages,
those non-Buddhists who are attached to a self constantly cultivate these various meditative absorptions.
All the assemblies of śrāvakas and likewise the pratyekabuddhas do the same.
Having thoroughly understood the self-characteristics of all phenomena in the world,
one sees that the aggregates and sense bases are like an empty house; herein there is no self,
no thought, and no activity, being like a mechanical corpse.
There is only the conjunction of the three; fundamentally, there is no agent.
Those non-Buddhists who practice meditative concentration give rise to the view of a fixed nature;
such people are deluded regarding the characteristics of phenomena and destroy all dharmas.
If there are those who can practice the subtle and wondrous samādhi of the Tathāgata, They will well understand that the aggregates are without self, and all views will be utterly extinguished.
All is but consciousness; the characteristics of all phenomena are entirely non-existent.
There is neither characteristic nor that which is characterized; there are no elements (*dhātu*) and no aggregates (*skandha*).
Even when analyzed down to the subtlest atom, none of these have any abiding place.
Earth, water, and all such things arise entirely from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Those who do not know its nature grasp at such signs—
whether of foul color or beautiful color— and the same applies to forms that resemble them or others.
It is like the various hues of clouds and rainbows appearing within the empty sky.
Contemplate [the body] as being like a skeleton, pervading the entire world;
likewise, through the meditations on the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), contemplate the great elements and so forth.
Whether the body possesses form or is formless, the one established in concentration should always contemplate it with discernment.
If one is single-minded regarding an object, that very object is said to be pure.
Just as it is conceptually discriminated, so does it become the focal object;
yet what is neither fixed nor fixed by nature is falsely imagined to be fixed.
The one established in meditative concentration, within that concentration, realizes that the world is entirely the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*);
phenomena and all characteristics of dharmas are all eliminated.
Having attained supreme concentration, they skillfully explain all forms of meditative absorption.
They destroy those who practice meditative concentration and the dharmas known through false wisdom.
If a person gives rise to inferior wisdom, grasping at dharmas and a self,
claiming their own words to be truthful and skillfully explaining all phenomena—
Fixated on the characteristics of all phenomena, one destroys oneself and others;
where there is no grasper nor grasped, one falsely gives rise to views of differentiation.
Sweetness can remove heat; bitterness, sourness, and saltiness stop phlegm.
Pungent substances transform cold; salt can cure wind-related ailments.
When phlegm and heat coexist within the body, they together give rise to malaria;
sometimes it arises solely from wind, or it originates from the combination of all three.
Because illnesses differ from one another, the skilled physician prescribes a multitude of remedies:
rock honey, the six-part compound, *yūṣa*, and various foods;
these can eliminate the various types of malarial fevers that afflict the bodies of sentient beings.
If phenomena possessed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),
then medicine would lack the power to eliminate disease, and the patient would not recover.
How is it that people in the world see the illness cured upon taking medicine?
The one established in meditative concentration observes that the world is nothing but the ālayavijñāna,
which undergoes transformation and flows on like various illusory animals.
There is neither the grasper nor the grasped, neither the aggregates nor the one who possesses the aggregates.
There is neither distinction of parts nor the possession of parts;
there is no creator in the world who creates the world,
nor is it a collection of atoms scattered throughout the ten directions.
It is not that the initial [atom] is most subtle, only to gradually become as large as a finger,
two fingers, or even three; nor is it that various objects combine and the *guṇas* (qualities) each differ— none of these doctrines hold true.
It does not arise at an improper time, nor from the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*), nor is it produced by the three factors, nor does it exist without a cause; rather, it comes to be spontaneously.
This is due to the habitual tendencies of karma (*karmavāsanā*) which disturb and cloud the inner mind.
Based on the mind and the eye-faculty, various false discriminations arise.
The mental faculty, the mental consciousness,
and the ālayavijñāna manifest throughout the world, like illusions creating all manner of things.
All objective realms, such as jars and the like, have the mind as their essence;
though they are not jars, they appear as jars, and for this reason they are said to be empty.
All forms existing in the world, such as the palaces of the various devas, [are likewise so].
All these are the ālayavijñāna, appearing through transformation.
Whatever belongs to the bodies of sentient beings— from the head down to the hands and feet—
whether arising all at once or in gradual succession, there is nothing that is not the ālayavijñāna.
Habitual tendencies turbid the mind; the foolish and ignorant cannot comprehend this.
This nature is neither existent, nor is it empty.
It is like a person who, with various objects, strikes and breaks a jar or the like.
If phenomena were empty, there would be neither subject nor object to be refuted.
Even a view of self as vast as Mount Sumeru is not considered evil;
yet to be conceited about one's attachment to emptiness—this evil exceeds that by far.
Emptiness should be taught according to what is appropriate; it should not be expounded where it is inappropriate.
If it is expounded where it is inappropriate, the nectar of immortality becomes poison.
All sentient beings give rise to various views.
Wishing to cause the severance of all views, he taught the principle of emptiness.
Yet hearing of emptiness, they grasped it as a substantial reality;
unable to sever their views, these views could not be removed, like a patient abandoned by a physician.
Just as fire burns wood, when the wood is exhausted the fire does not remain;
when the wood is seen as already burnt, the fire of emptiness should likewise be extinguished.
When the fire of wisdom arises and all views are extinguished, [the fire of emptiness also ceases].
Universally incinerating all afflictions, All things become utterly pure;
By means of this wisdom, the Muni Is liberated within the Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha).
One does not see a rabbit’s horn Touching and destroying a great mountain.
Never has there been a stone-child who, grasping an arrow, shot at an object;
nor have we ever heard of one wishing to engage in battle while seeking a bow made of rabbit horns.
Who, moreover, would require a palace and command a stone-child to build it?
The emptiness of all phenomena is eternally of one essence with those phenomena;
from the moment of conception in the womb, as form arises, it immediately perishes.
Apart from emptiness there is no form, and apart from form there is no emptiness.
Just as the moon and its radiance are never different from beginning to end, so too are all phenomena: emptiness is one with them.
As they are mutually indistinguishable, all that is undertaken is successfully accomplished.
This body is like a corpse; from the beginning it lacks intrinsic nature.
Constantly bound by the ropes of craving, it is pulled and moved by sensory objects.
The Buddha taught the principle of emptiness in order to sever all views.
You who possess wisdom, you should study with single-minded devotion.
Just as a skilled illusionist, through the power of various incantations and arts,
creates whatever he desires from conditions such as grass and wood.
Depending upon the eye, craving, attention, forms, and light, visual consciousness arises;
it is like a magical illusion and like a mirage.
This consciousness has no place from which it comes, nor does it have any destination where it goes.
The nature of all consciousnesses is thus; one should not cling to existence or non-existence.
Like the son of a barren woman, the horns of a rabbit, or a mass of floating hairs, they originally lack any substantial essence and are merely established through false designations.
Lions, bears, and brown bears—none of these have horns.
Why do you not distinguish this, speaking only of the non-existence of rabbit horns?
O you who are skilled in discourse, could you not explain this?
The wise sages of antiquity spoke only of the hare having no horns;
those who are deluded engage in false discrimination, like the mute, the deaf, and the blind.
Such people lack present wisdom and cannot personally realize the Dharma for themselves.
If one merely follows the shifting words of others, what is the use of making distinctions?
If one is free from such discrimination, one shall be born in the Land of Secret Adornment;
within single-minded right concentration, one will universally manifest throughout the lands of the ten directions.
Just as the celestial palaces, the various stars,
and the sun and moon depend upon Mount Sumeru and are sustained and moved by the power of the wind,
so too are the seven consciousnesses dependent upon the ālayavijñāna.
Sustained by habitual tendencies, one constantly transmigrates from place to place.
Just as the great earth gives rise to all manner of things—every sentient being and even all kinds of precious jewels; so too does the mind give rise to all phenomena.
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is likewise the support for all the various consciousnesses.
Just as the peacock bird has feathers of many brilliant colors,
and male and female love one another, dancing and sporting together in joy.
The meditator who contemplates the ālayavijñāna should know it is likewise:
seeds and all phenomena abide in mutual dependence upon one another.
Just as the myriad rivers flow day and night toward the great ocean, so do they all return to the storehouse consciousness.
The flowing stream never ceases, and the ocean makes no distinctions;
so too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), profound and boundless,
into which the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of all the cognitions constantly flow day and night.
Just as the earth contains various jewels and other diverse things,
providing for all sentient beings according to their respective needs,
so too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which coexists with all forms of discrimination.
Increasing within birth and death, one transforms the basis to achieve perfect enlightenment.
Practicing wholesome and pure conduct, one transcends the ten stages and enters the stage of the Tathāgata, wherein the ten powers are all perfected.
Abiding correctly in the limit of reality, Eternal and never subject to destruction,
Like the earth, free from discrimination, His manifestations and transformations are inexhaustible.
Like the myriad flowers blooming in spring, Which both humans and birds joyfully admire.
The appropriating consciousness is likewise; those in meditative concentration are often deluded by grasping.
Such sons of the Buddhas, lacking wisdom and separated from reality, do not properly understand the meaning and thus give rise to dogmatic assertions through false speech.
With unrighteous divisive speech, they delude and confuse sentient beings;
though all phenomena abide in their distinctness, they give rise to separate discourses.
It is like a skilled illusionist who is adept at employing incantations.
Where there are no flowers or fruits, they manifest various kinds of flowers and fruits.
In this way, through the wisdom of skillful means,
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwell in the world in diverse ways and establish themselves in diverse ways.
He expounds various gates of teaching, Instructing and guiding without end;
The definitive and true Dharma Is manifested within the *Ghanavyūha*.
The six elements and eighteen, The twelve bases and the person (*puruṣa*),
Drawn by the tether of the mind, sentient beings wander through saṃsāra.
The eight consciousnesses, the various elements, and the sense bases arise together in harmony;
driven by the tether of the mind, they pass from a former body to a subsequent body.
“The Buddha has taught that this person (puruṣa) flows along with the causes of the world;
as this embodied being, he continues through successive births without interruption.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha had explained the meaning of the person in relation to the elements (dhātu) and sense-bases (āyatana), all the great Bodhisattvas who had attained fearlessness within the pure palace of the Maṇi-ratna treasury came forward and prostrated themselves in homage.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable multitudes of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who had come to this assembly from various lands, and they praised in unison, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!

Within the assembly, there were also immeasurable Bodhisattvas, devas, and celestial maidens, all of whom rose from their seats, stood with palms joined, looked upon one another, and spoke these verses:
"Among all those established in meditative concentration, you alone are the foremost.
Now, for the sake of the bodhisattvas, you speak of the subtle and wondrous Great Man,
who remains far removed from non-Buddhists and their attachment to theories of selfhood."
As you have proclaimed, O Noble One, the Puruṣa who is pure in the six elements is merely a combination of these elements, flowing according to causes.
It is like the tracks of a bird clearly appearing in the sky.
Just as fire might blaze up apart from wood,
or as the tracks of a bird might appear in the sky— fire existing independently of wood—
I and all the world have never seen such a thing.
As a bird flies upon its wings, leaving no trace in the sky,
so too is the "person" spoken of by the Benevolent One similar to a bird's track; how,
then, can there be the principle of saṃsāra within the various realms of existence?

Yet it is said that the person (pudgala) within the realms constantly transmigrates through birth and death, experiencing the fruits of various suffering and pleasure; how is it that the karma one has performed is never lost?
Just as when a farmer performs his labor, he never fails to obtain the fruit.
Once this fruit has ripened, a subsequent fruit shall arise again.
It is the same for the person: by dwelling in the body and practicing wholesome deeds, one will constantly enjoy the pleasures of gods and humans in both present and future lives.
Some constantly cultivate merit and virtue, taking these provisions as the cause for Buddhahood;
through liberation and the various perfections, they attain perfect enlightenment.
As for the fruit of sovereign rebirth in heaven, through contemplative practice one perceives the true meaning.
If one were apart from the person (pudgala), nothing at all would exist.
Because there is a person who transmigrates within the cycle of birth and death,
from the Avīci Hell below up to the realms of the gods above.
This karma will inevitably produce its fruit; what is done is never in vain.
Whether internal or external, within the world, things arise through mutual power;
this phenomenon resembles that, and that arises from this.
Although one may be free from the realms of existence, there are those who still undergo saṃsāra.
It is like saying that a woman born of a stone performs graceful gestures and advances or retreats;
or that the horns of a rabbit are sharp and piercing; or that oil can be extracted from sand.

At that time, after the bodhisattvas, devas, and devīs in the assembly had spoken these words, they all together made offerings to the Worthy One who is worthy of offerings, the Venerable Vajragarbha, and all the bodhisattvas.
Having completed the offerings, they again spoke these verses with one mind:
“The Dharma-eye is complete and without defect; Both causes and analogies are fully adorned.
Able to subdue the arguments of others, It reveals the virtues of our own school.”
"Therefore, O Greatly Diligent One, you should swiftly expound this.
The devas and humans in this assembly all desire to hear it with single-minded devotion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha replied in verse:
"This Dharma is profound and difficult to conceive; it cannot be reached by discursive thought.
The principle of pure yoga is unfolded through causes and metaphors.
Within the realm of Śrī-māyādhāra where meditative concentration is cultivated, I proclaim it."
“You all, gods and humans, should listen with one mind.
Having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha then addressed the Great Tree Kinnara King with these verses:
“Great Tree Kinnara, you should know the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).”
How do all phenomena abide?
Their nature is empty and devoid of anything existent; seeing them thus in accordance with reality, one will not be deluded regarding meditative concentration.
Just as when a single grain of rice is cooked, the state of the remaining grains can be known.
All phenomena are likewise so; by knowing one, one knows them all.
Just as one who churns curd tastes it with the tip of a finger, so too can the nature of all phenomena be observed through a single point.
The nature of phenomena is neither existent, nor is it empty;
it is a transformation of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), and the storehouse takes emptiness as its characteristic.
At that time, the King of the Great Tree Kiṃnaras asked in verse:
"How can there be realms and persons within the measure of mind?
How do the various realms arise—with solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion?
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha replied in verse:
“Excellent, Great King of Trees! That you now ask such a question is intended to cause practitioners to direct their minds toward the ultimate reality.
I shall now speak for your sake; O master lute-player, you should listen well.”
In the past, you mounted a celestial palace together with your entire retinue;
accompanied by the sound of drums and music, you descended from the sky and came to the place where the Buddha was.
The lute played upon your hands was adorned with lapis lazuli.
The sounds of the lute were harmonious and elegant, delighting and moving the hearts of the multitude.
The immeasurable śrāvakas, who were observing and listening in the presence of the Buddha, could no longer maintain their original resolve; each rose up and began to dance.
Then the Great Being Tiānguān addressed Kāśyapa and the others, saying:
"You who have abandoned desire, why do you dance and play?
At that time, Mahākāśyapa replied to that Great Being Tiānguān:
The Bodhisattva possesses great power, like a whirlwind;
the Śrāvaka lacks definitive wisdom, like a black mountain being shaken.
Though they have abandoned deluded discrimination, they remain stained by the mud of habitual tendencies.
Having abandoned all habitual tendencies, with a pure mind you shall become a Buddha.
Regarding subtle objects, your mind has already attained penetration;
amidst the various worldly discourses, you are clear and decisive.
You are skilled in the characteristics of all the stages and in the pure dharmas of the Buddhas.
Seated within your palace, surrounded by your retinue,
you are pure and magnificent, like the full moon at its peak.
Able, amidst the assembly of those who have attained mastery in the cultivation of contemplative practice, you ask me, the Great Being of the Realms: "How does it arise from the mind?
You and all the sons of the Buddhas should now listen with a single-minded focus.
Just as within the various elements, the mind is called the "Great Man" (puruṣa), and all elements arise because of it—I shall now explain this meaning.
Moisture gives rise to water; heat gives rise to fire.
The movement of all karmic actions gives rise to the element of wind;
from the demarcation of form, there arise earth and space.
Through objective spheres and habitual tendencies, consciousness arises and coalesces.
"The eye and its objects, such as forms, etc., have distinct and differing characteristics.
These constitute the gateway for birth, wherein all states of existence perpetually continue.

At that time, in the Palace of Sovereign Mani-Jewel Treasury, the Bodhisattva Dharinivardhana, together with immeasurable bodhisattvas, rose from his seat, prostrated himself in salutation, and presented various exquisite offerings to the Venerable Vajragarbha.
Furthermore, they spread jeweled nets to completely cover it above, praising with one voice, "Excellent!
Excellent! and spoke these verses:
“The Venerable One abides in the Dharma-cloud stage, having skillfully entered the Buddha-ground;
he is able to reveal and explain the realm of the Tathāgata to all bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Kinnara King Mahādruma, together with his many court ladies, again presented various kinds of exquisite offerings as an act of worship.
Having completed the offerings, he praised him with these verses:
“Excellent, Vajragarbha, you who have attained fearlessness!
For our sake, you have expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata.”
"Now this maṇi-palace is pure and most auspicious.

At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Ratnaśikhin Bodhisattva, Devamukuṭa Bodhisattva, Dhāraṇīśvara Bodhisattva, Sarvārthasiddha Bodhisattva, and other such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as immeasurable other practitioners of contemplation—all of whom were sons of the Buddha possessing great majesty and virtue, and who were well-able to reveal the mind of contemplative practice—rose from their seats, looked at one another, and addressed the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Vajragarbha in verse, saying:
"We pray that the Vajra Honored One Will manifest the Eye of Dharma."
The Venerable One’s marks of excellence, He comprehends and knows them all;
The Tathāgata constantly remembers and upholds him, And he is revered by the Sons of the Buddha.
Now this assembly of great power, With one mind, makes this request.
O Master of Yoga, we pray that you reveal this in the Guhyasamāja; may all worlds everywhere attain what has never been known before.
This Dharma is most pure and transcends all verbal expression;
it has not yet been expounded in the sūtras by the transformation Buddhas or the Bodhisattvas.
The noble ones experience the bliss of the present life;
They perceive the true, untainted realm, The domain of self-awakened wisdom, Pure and most incomparable.
They are fully endowed with all samādhis As well as dhāraṇīs.
The various masteries and liberations, the ten kinds of mind-made bodies,
the adornment and purification of Buddha-lands in inconceivable numbers,
and the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose physical dimensions are like motes of dust—
Even as one part in a hundred of a hair-tip,
so is the Land of Śrī-vaśavartin among all lands; most excellent,
those practitioners who contemplate thus will be reborn in this realm.
"What is the cause of all this?
O Son of the Buddha, we pray that you will explain it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, [spoke:]
Adorning his body, desiring to proclaim the primordial Buddha-eye that is non-conceptual and free from discrimination,
he surveys the entire assembly like a lion king; knowing that their intellectual power is capable of receiving and upholding [the teaching],
he utters with a Brahma-voice, a kalaviṅka-like voice, and the pure, beautiful sound of the broad and long tongue— a voice that is definitive.
It is pleasing to all, free from coarseness, refined, gentle, and clear;
it is fully endowed with immeasurable virtues corresponding to the *kinnara* voice, the *udātta* voice, the *sittila* voice, the *riṣabha* voice, the *pañcama* voice, and the *vairamitradhura* voice.

He does not cause the minds of those who hear him to become deluded or attached; he is skillfully able to thoroughly comprehend the characteristics of sounds, so that all devas, humans, gandharvas, and others do not fail to rejoice.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha was without verbal speech; yet, by the power of his original vow, from his body—specifically from his eyebrows, forehead, crown, nose, and even down to his shoulders and knees—such sounds issued forth spontaneously, like a magical transformation, as he expounded the Eye of the Dharma for the great assembly.
Just as a king of geese, surrounded by a flock of geese, appears pure, bright, and magnificent upon a sandy bank,

so too does the Greatly Diligent Vajragarbha abide in his sovereign, pure palace, surrounded by the assembly of all Buddha-sons, appearing equally pure and magnificent— like the bright moon in the sky illuminating the host of stars.

The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha is likewise; seated upon the lion throne, he outshines all others. Just as there is no distinction between the moon and its light, so too is there no difference between the Buddha and the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha; they are equal and indistinguishable.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Yathārthadarśin, who was the foremost among the assembly dwelling on the stage of practice, rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, gazed upon the Bodhisattvas, and spoke these verses:
“Alas! The Mahāyāna Dharma, Subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable— The realm of the Tathāgata, To which the sons of the Buddha should pay homage.”
The thought-free and stainless Dharma is rare and extremely difficult to encounter.
Throughout all lands, it is that which all Buddhas observe:
the true meaning of the Mahāyāna, pure and beyond compare.
Far removed from all conceptual constructions, it is the sublime path of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
The spheres of the eight consciousnesses, the various distinct natures,
the five dharmas, and selflessness— these are revealed through their differentiation.
Enshrouded by the five kinds of habitual tendencies, one gives rise to various evil discriminations.
Seeing this subtle and wondrous Dharma, which is as pure as genuine gold,
those who attain this purity immediately abide in the Buddha-lineage.
The nature of the Tathāgata is subtle and wondrous; among all lands, neither non-Buddhists nor śrāvakas can equal the Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha), which is supreme.
Having perfected their spiritual lineage, they come to be born in this land.
"Venerable Vajragarbha, what samādhi have you already attained?
What is the samādhi that constitutes the realm of these pure dharmas you have spoken?
At that time, there was an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas in the gathering who, having prostrated with their heads to the ground, spoke in verse:
"O Vajragarbha of Great Wisdom, we pray that you will explain for us:
abiding in what samādhi are you able to preach this Dharma?
All these sons of the Buddha likewise desire to hear it."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, who possesses great fearlessness, surveyed the entire assembly with the power of his wisdom to determine whether they were capable of receiving and upholding this inconceivable Dharma, or not.
Having observed them closely, knowing that these sons of the Buddha were capable of receiving this Dharma, he spoke these verses:
"You sons of the Buddha, all of you should listen with a single mind;
I shall now explain for you the wondrous path of the transformation of the basis."
The samādhi that I have attained Is named "Majestic Power of the Mahāyāna.
When Bodhisattvas dwell within it, They are able to expound the pure Dharma,
And they also behold all the Tathāgatas Within billions of lands.
Countless as the sands of the Ganges, nayutas in number, stood before him and praised:
"Excellent is what you have spoken! This is the path of yoga;
we, all the Tathāgatas, have all practiced this samādhi."
Attaining mastery therein, one becomes pure and realizes perfect enlightenment.
There has never been a single Buddha who was not born from this samādhi;
therefore, this samādhi cannot be fathomed by mere thought.
If there are bodhisattvas who dwell within this samādhi,
they immediately abide in the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas.
They realize the sphere of their own wisdom and behold all the Buddhas.
Manifesting hundreds of thousands of billions of transformations, even as subtle as motes of dust;
the wondrous principle of inner realization is that wherein all Buddhas abide.
This Dharma is devoid of all marks and is far removed from sound and form.
Names arise from signs; signs arise from causes and conditions.
These two give rise to conceptual discrimination. The nature of all phenomena is suchness (tathatā);
to observe this skillfully is called right knowledge.
What is called "imagined nature" (parikalpita-svabhāva) is the characteristic (lakṣaṇa), which is the "dependent origination" (paratantra-svabhāva).
When both name and characteristic are discarded, this is the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) dwells within the body and flows and wanders according to its circumstances.
Habitual tendencies are piled up like mountains, entangled by the defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*).
The *manas* has two gates, arising simultaneously with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
as the five objects appear before one, the various bodies of consciousness merge in harmony.
Just as there is a self and a person, dwelling within the body,
so too the torrential stream of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), tossed by the winds of objective realms,
gives rise to various waves of cognition that flow on in succession without ever ceasing.
The Buddhas and the various Bodhisattvas, being able to know the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya),
have already attained the state of Tathāgata and further proclaim it for the sake of others.
By analyzing the aggregates (skandha), they perceive the nature of the selflessness of persons (pudgalanairātmya).
Not knowing that there are no phenomena, these are called śrāvakas.
The bodhisattva is well able to contemplate the two kinds of selflessness— of persons and of phenomena— and having contemplated them,
he immediately relinquishes them, not dwelling even in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
If one dwells in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one would abandon the mind of great compassion;
all meritorious deeds would remain unaccomplished, and one could not attain perfect enlightenment.
It is through rare and inconceivable wisdom that all sentient beings are universally benefited.
Just as a lotus emerges from the mud, its form and color exceedingly majestic and pure,
so that all devas and noble beings, upon seeing it, give rise to love and reverence; likewise,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emerge from the mire of birth and death.
The body of the Buddha is pure, Admired and venerated by all devas.
From the initial stage of a bodhisattva, He may become a wheel-turning monarch,
A lord of devas, an asura, Or a gandharva king, and so forth.
Those who realize the Mahāyāna obtain such a body as this;
by practicing the path gradually, they will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Therefore, all you sons of the Buddha, you should study with a single-minded resolve.
All sentient beings in the world, and all phenomena such as defilement and purity, depend upon the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as their cause for arising.
This cause is supreme and peerless; those who have realized the truth have proclaimed it.
It is not similar to a creator, such as Īśvara or others.
The World-Honored One taught this consciousness in order to eliminate all habitual tendencies;
once liberation is fully realized, even this [consciousness] is found to be unobtainable.
The ālayavijñāna is subject to attainment, and liberation is not eternal;
the Tathāgata’s pure storehouse is also called stainless wisdom,
eternally abiding without beginning or end, transcending the discourse of the four extremes.
The Buddha taught that the Tathāgatagarbha is the ālaya;
those of evil intelligence cannot know it, for the Garbha is the ālayavijñāna.
The Tathāgata’s pure Garbha is the worldly ālaya.
Just as gold and a finger-ring are mutually indistinguishable;
for example, like a skilled goldsmith who, using pure and excellent refined gold,
fashions an ornament for the finger, desiring thereby to adorn the finger.
Its characteristic differs from all other things, and thus it is called a "finger-ring.
The noble ones who manifest bliss realize the domain of their own wisdom;
their merit increases ever more excellently, such that neither self-nature nor commonality can describe it.
Those who practice meditative concentrations in the present life realize that objects are nothing but consciousness;
having attained the seventh stage, these [conceptions] are transformed and extinguished so as not to arise again.
All objective spheres are merely the movements of the mind and consciousness.
Although what is perceived appears to be differentiated, consciousness alone exists and no external objects do.
Objects such as jars, garments, and other things are entirely non-existent;
it is the transformation of the mind that arises resembling objects, which we designate as the grasper and the grasped.
Just as the stars and the moon move in dependence upon Mount Sumeru,
so too do all consciousnesses constantly revolve in dependence upon the ālaya.
Know that this ālayavijñāna is precisely what is called Ghanavyūha.
Just as fine, genuine gold is always replete with radiant color, so too is the realm of self-realization pure; it is not a sphere of conceptual discrimination.
Its nature is free from discrimination and cannot be conceptually differentiated.
Its essence is real and eternal; those who are concentrated are able to perceive it.
It is the objective sphere traversed by the mental consciousness;
it merely binds the ordinary person, yet to the vision of the noble ones, it is entirely pure, like a mirage and the like.

When the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra, the immeasurable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas such as Vajragarbha, along with the countless multitudes who had come from other directions to this assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra on the Secret Adornment, Scroll II.
